Institute of Jazz Studies
Conducted by Preston Love
October 31, 1981

S. & S. REPORTING CO., INC.
Court Reporters—Notaries

Ernie Fields, the great bandleader from the southwest, based at Tulsa, Oklahoma.
First Ernie, I started asking you where you were born, when and how it all began with you.
Okay, let's go, Preston.

I was born in Nacogdoches, Texas, Sunday at midnight, August 28, 1904. Reverend Thomas Jefferson Fields was my father and Mary Jane Garrett Fields, mother. The baby of the family of three boys and two girls. The family moved to an all black town, Taft, Oklahoma, 1905. At that time, indian territory.
My father was killed accidentally in 1906. I was known as Sonny Boy before school age and until the fifth grade while going to school.
After sixth grade I finally decided I had to have a name, and all of them kidding me--the youngsters--that my people didn't
think enough of me to name me. I always said, well, they wanted me to be sure that I was satisfied with it.

Then, it came out in the Muskogee daily paper, no more Sonny Boy Fields, it's now Ernie Lawrence Fields. I was a very popular kid, but both the boys and girls used to kid me-- I already said that, but they can edit that-- about not having any name, my parents not naming me. My answer was always they wanted to be sure that I had a name that I would be satisfied with. They demanded that I have the honor of naming myself.

I was from a musical family. As a kid--by being the baby--the nearest one to me was twelve years older than me, so you understand, I was really the baby. And seemingly, although a poor family, they, by losing my father, they were determined that I wouldn't want for anything, and all along they're just human; but I don't think they spoiled me by doing it, but as I said, I didn't know anything at all
about hard times, although we had nothing. And I never was known to be hungry, although we had nothing.
As I got older I wondered a lot of times how in the world my mother even managed to get along with what little we did, trying to farm around.

They wouldn't take me out of school to do any kind of work; whatever I did it had to be after school. As I said, the family, the two girls both played piano and the boys had a little singing quartet and they would sing around. I got a very big kick out of it, but never, never dreamed that I would be--that that would be my livelihood, and at that time, as a kid, they would have the little country picnics and they would have somebody playing, maybe one horn or guitar or piano up on a wooden platform, and I would walk miles to hear that which I enjoyed but looked like no bug was on me to really learn how to play anything.
That was in Nacogdoches?
No, that was in Tulsa; that was in Taft, Oklahoma. I might have missed a point. My family moved to Oklahoma when I was maybe a little less than a year old, and I never did even know my father.
You moved there in your infancy?
Yes, during my infancy.
In Taft?

Taft, Oklahoma. A black town, an all colored town nine miles from Muskogee. That was the largest town near. Later on, I will get to it, Muskogee played a big part in my career too. But anyway, I would walk and walk to hear these things, so finally my sister began to say, you like music so, why don't you learn to do something yourself. So I began to play piano. But as I got older, I fell in a little with baseball, and that was my dream, to be a
big league baseball player. All through junior high school I was playing good in everything but running. No coach or teacher could teach me to run, I couldn't run.

So anyway, as things went on, a young lady, Eva Jessye, was the first to ever teach me--besides my sister--on the piano. She was one of the teachers, and she was a vocal teacher, and she went on a little later to fame. She left Taft and came to New York and worked and had the Eva Jessye Choir, and now she's known as Dr. Eva Jessye. As of right now, I tried to contact her to get some points before I came up here, she's in some capacity at the University of Kansas--Kansas State College in Pittsburgh. She's now, I think, eighty something years old.
Her name is Eva--
Dr. Eva Jessye.
And that was my first real music teacher. And I don't know why she thought that I should sing, but in some ways, during her

training, my voice was changing, and it looked like I couldn't get things right, and I just dwelled in myself, that oh, I can't sing. And so we laughed about that later on after I met her, because she left the area and went on for years and years, and then I went to travel as a band.
She came to see me, my first trip at the Apollo Theatre in New York City, and she was saying how nice it was, but why wasn't I singing something. And I told her I never could sing.

That was really my first real teacher. But I still wanted to go away and as I said, I never did think about music as a livelihood, and I wanted to be an auto mechanic; baseball and auto mechanic was my dream. I could just listen to the old cars and tell you what was wrong by the sound it was making.
So I decided I wanted to go away to training school and not having money to pay my way and I always heard that you could work

your way in Tuskegee. So my brother had been to Tuskegee and was out. Of course he was a little different from me, me went to take the trumpet around Taft from some teacher that came in and he had been in the Tuskegee student band and was a very fine musician all the way. He left Tuskegee--Tuskegee didn't have a college department at that time, but he went on, I think to state college, and majored in music. But I wasn't even thinking about it, making music, my mind was on auto mechanics.

I never know why the change came in, but when I entered Tuskegee, well somewhere applied electricity came around and I decided I wanted to be an electrician, and after that my brother kidded me a long time and said, I guess I must have thought I didn't want to get big.
Anyway, I started school in Tuskegee, but before that, I was trying to figure out how was I going to go to school. There was a fellow with the railroad that had a section

gang and I heard, as a youngster, that he wanted to hire some extra people, and there were still a lot of the oldtimers calling me Sonny Boy, and I went to see Roy Martin, the section hand foreman, and told him I wanted a job, that school was out and he said, what can you do, Sonny Boy? I said I--
How old were you then?
I was around seventeen, I guess, maybe sixteen.

Then he said, there's nothing you can do. And I said next year when I come out of school, I want to go to Tuskegee, I want to learn a trade, I want to go to Tuskegee, and he said there's nothing you can do. I continue to talk, and he said, come back and see me, on your nerve, I might pick out something.

So I went to see him again and he said the extra gang is coming in, there's a strip of track we have to finish out, and with as many men as I have working, I'll need a water boy, and he said I'll make you a water boy and
then in between you can cut weeds. He gave me one of them blades to go and cut weeds.

So I went to work and it seemed like all the section gang, they were nailing rails and this and that, and when I started to cut weeds, they'd say water boy, you ought to bring that here, so I'd get the water and go around to them and everything. Well, that played out.

I would save the little month that I was making and everything, but I had practically a year to make up, because I was trying to figure ahead. So my mother says, well, what are you going to do. One of my sister's were married and lived in Muskogee and so, I said I'm going and live with Jo, and I'll get me a job doing so and so; shining shoes, if nothing else.
So I went to Muskogee and got a job in a shining parlor, and of course, I never will forget, my mother saying, son, whatever you do, do it good. But as a country boy, I
didn't know there were but three kinds of shoes, that is, white shoes, black shoes and tan shoes, but still, I'm going to work in one of them shine parlors.

One day I was shining a man's shoes, he had on tan shoes, and I was just shining the heels, I was going to make them shine like the toe, and all the boys that worked there, they began to laugh, and they would say little words, this and that, and I didn't know what they were talking about, so when they got through and the man handed me a nickel, and everybody fell out laughing, and all but one boy, and that boy was Walter Thomas. He said, we tried to tell you, and the guys would say, you're lucky, you got a nickel. You wasted all that time, that man will never give nothing; they'd goof on me. I said you got to tell me, and he took me aside, and told me all the old names, what they mean, the guys that had been working there, they knew how to work for a nickel, a dime, and you're never going to get a quarter in those

days, and so I thanked him and as time went on we became kind of buddy-buddy and he says maybe Saturday we're going to do this and I'd say, no, I'm saving my money. He say, what are you so tight for; I'd say I'm trying to save money to go to Tuskegee. And he said, that's what I'm working for, I'm going to some school up in Topeka, training school. He said that's where I'm going to school.
KVS.
What?
Kansas Vocational School.
Yes. That's where he said he's going to school.

So we were just good buddies along and everything. When that was over, I went on then to finish school, a junior, and so that summer, before going to school, I came to Tulsa, my brother was teaching in Sand Springs, and I decided then that I was going to come up there and my mother said yes, she'll go up and stay
with my brother, so I got me a job dishwashing in Bishop's Cafe. At that time, that was one of the big cafe's in Tulsa.

At first we had a big discussion about going up there and now you've got to be careful, that was just after the riot. They had this big riot in Tulsa, and so after talking to my brother, you know that's all over anyway, you can't stop, the world is going on anyway. That's just one of those things, it might happen if you're there or if you're not.
Are you referring to the big race riot?
In Tulsa, Oklahoma.
In what year?
Either seventeen or eighteen.
You went afterwards?
Yes, I went afterwards, and of course my mother thought about that and was one of them, well actually I should not even be away from home.

And so anyway, my brother went on, and while I was working there, while I was a dishwasher--well actually, I did not go in the dining room, but after a while the busboy would (inaudible). So this guy, I don't know where he was from, he didn't know what to call it, I don't know what kind of name they called that orchestra, but finally I said to them, I'll tell you what, when I get through I'm going to help you get your dishes out of the dining room. He said okay. I got through with mine right quick and I said man, that's an orchestra. He said I didn't know what you were talking about.
This orchestra was playing at Bishops?
Yes.
A black one?
No, it was white.
And so then this was the most beautiful music that I heard. That little country music around Taft and Muskogee, but I never heard anything like that and they had violins
and everything and horns. I would always rush. Then we got to be pretty tight, this busboy, and he would help me and I'd get through and then I'd help him get his dishes.
In the dining room?
Yes; so I could hang around the dining room and hear the band.

So we went on for a little longer and that next fall I did go to Tuskegee, and so after I enrolled I was in the Registrar's office and one of the members--I forget what capacity he was in--but was Wilson, the father of Teddy Wilson, was in this office when I was registering myself, and of course during those days, they had a big oil boom and to sell Oklahomans (inaudible) was there, and when I gave where I was from, the guy says, Captain Neely it was known as, and there were two people from Oklahoma who had a very good reputation who was Jake Simmons and my brother, Clarence Fields. They were older and they were known--around 1920 or something--and everybody remembered them,

and so anyway, they guy said, what are you, are you going to be like the other two. Did you come here just to spend some of your money. I said no, I said I'm asking you now, all I have is my entrance fee and I'm coming here to work my way through school, and he said you Oklahomans don't need anything. I said what are you talking about. So they opened the door and when they opened the door, there was at least three guys back there who were sleeping, and so they had had them in there for something, they'd been into or something, and they didn't care, they were sleeping, and so they woke them up and so I asked them where they were from and thye were from Haskell, Oklahoma, not so far away.

The thing was these were what we called natives. They had money and got into something and were very careless around. Anyway, I entered school and went onto school and everything was going on there and then nicely and then when I'd get to hear the orchestra, to go into the dining room, and that band, the Tuskegee
Band, I said I've got to play some kind of horn. It went to the band director, Captain Dryer--
Now, at Tuskegee?
Yes.
They had a band too at the restaurant?
Yes, in our dining room, the orchestra played, then they had the marching band, the big band. They had a big band.

So Captain Dryer was the band director and so I went to see Captain Dryer and I told him I'd like to get in the second band. I said I know a little about music and he said that's fine, what horn, what do you want to play and I said I want to play anything, I just want to play. He started laughing and he said that's all right, but what horn do you have? I said (inaudible).
Anyway, he was very nice and he said I hope you can figure out something. He

went on, and he said, my goodness, I remember your brother here. Why in the world didn't Clarence make you get a horn before you came here or something. So we went on and one of my classmates, Owens--
Wait a minute. What was the band director's name again?
Frank L. Dryer.
Dryer?
YES. D-R-Y-E-R.
That's Tuskegee?
That's Tuskegee.

So, I got to talking with Owens, my classmate, who was a trumpet player, and I said, I sure wish I could be in that band. He called and asked a few questions about music and he said you know a little bit and I said, I had one or two lessons on the piano, but I was too lazy to practice and this and that, but I want a horn. So he finally said what kind of

horn and I told him just like I said to Captain Dryer. I said any instrument, but I want to get in that band. He said I'll look around. So one day he came to me and said, Ernie, Ernie, I said what, there's this band--there's this trombone that he wants to sell and I said I don't have--and he said he'll sell it cheap, he just wants some money, he's broke and he wants some money. So he took me to this guy and this guy said yeah, I'll sell you the trombone. I said what do you want for it; he said six dollars. I said I don't have six dollars; you don't even have six dollars, I'm almost giving it to you. I said no, I don't have no six dollars; what do you have? And so I said I have three dollars, and he said (inaudible), but I'm going to let you have it for the three, but now you owe me three dollars. So I told him okay, and so I took the trombone.
So I went to Captain Dryer, he said well, you have a horn, but you can't use this. I'll tell you what, Fields,seeing that

you're determined and I am going to send this out to be repaired, and I thanked him, and so he sent the horn away and when it came back it was in pretty nice shape and all and then I went to go in the second band, starting from the beginning and taking lessons in the second. band.
That was the latter part of the year. About the middle of the year when I got the horn--it was the latter part of the school term.
Exactly what year did you enroll at the school?
It was twenty.
Yes.
And that was about the middle of it.
(Inaudible)
a clarinet player, a very fine musician and by me working up my way and everything, I was staying--I wasn't coming home then, so I was going to work all that summer
and I would continue my schooling that next fall.
What were you studying now?
Applied electricity. I wanted to be in the band but no music was connected as my livelihood.
Your major was electricity?

Yeah, that's it. So he says, I tell you what, he was on the second band, if you could get assigned to work with me this summer at the power plant, we would change dynamos, work so many hours and then we cleaned it off and this and that, and changed the dynamo over for the next twenty four hours, and he said if you work with me down there, what we will do is drill. He said I'll drill you three or four hours every morning and before we go to bed.
So I talked to the electrical instructor and told him I wasn't going home and

would he assign me with Moore--William Moore-- and so he told me yes he would, and so Moore and I would come in and he would take his clarinet, because he could transpose, and work along with me and everything. He would tell me I'm coming along and I would practice and so when school started I was in the band--they put me in the band, and I still had this horn that he had repaired.
The Captain had his eye on me and so along about the middle of that school term he says I got a surprise for you, and so he called me up to his office and had a brand new Conn.
A Conn trombone?
Yes.
He moved me up to second bone and he said I knew that all you needed was something to play.
And so then I was on my way and (inaudible) we were started to get together with each other and play around and do you remember
Yeah, Lunsford.
Well, he was in the band. Stevens was his last name, I can't think of his first name.
He got killed in the service, didn't he?
He may have. I don't remember.
But he was the high man with Lunsford.

Well, his home is Tuskegee and he meant a lot to me, a little competition between us and Hawkins, was at Alabama State at Montgomery and they began to talk about him, so we were trying to have a little group to outdo Erskine Hawkins down at Alabama State.

So anyway, as I said, Tuskegee is really a ROTC department and so we had this uniform and all, and now me being in the electrical department, I'm supposed to know, which I did, we had a special place where you had to
x Tommy Stevenson

have the proper wattage for you to press. For you to iron anything, you got no business ironing anything in your room, so we were getting ready to make up a parade or something and I'm going to be all sharp in uniform, and I was in the room pressing, and we had a guy, we all called him the biggest snitch, he was the captain's stoolie in ROTC and he looked like he could slip--
Captain who?
Stock--he was the captain in the ROTC.
Was he a student?
Yes, he was a student.

And so Stock, what's the matter now, what's the smell, somethings going on in there, and so he knocked on my door and he didn't know exactly who it was and he goes and finds out exactly who was in the room. So he came back and said, Fields, I know it's you, open up, I smell you pressing in there, I smell that wool. So I opened the door and I

told Stock, I said don't tell anybody, what difference is it going to make, I'm trying to look a little decent for this parade and he goes anybody ought to know, you're an electrician and you're in here pressing in your room. You might set the building on fire, you got no business. So he turned me in and so they called me up to the office and they said what in the world, you're an electrician and you're in there pressing, I suspect you're the one who helped fix up the place with the proper wiring. He said well, I'll tell you what, we have to suspend you for at least a week, we can't look over you, you have a nice record and everything, but we have to make an example, we don't have any pets here, and so you're going to have to go home and they tried to make it like a little vacation, they said, you haven't been home since you've been here, have you?
Now when they suspended you, they would send you home?
Yeah, that's what

they're supposed to do. So I said, I can't go home, I don't have any money. Can't you send home for money? I said my mother is a widow and I'm trying to work my way here. Well, you've got to do something, and so they said you've got to get off the campus for a week.

So I told Captain Dryer and so he said don't worry, I think Steve has a big house, hell, his people will let you stay. So when I talked to Steve, he said oh, don't worry about a thing and he laughed and we all had a big laugh and he went and made arrangements with his people that I could stay there for a week and he went and told them that they were suspending me for a week, that I didn't do anything disgraceful but I had to be off the campus.

At first they said two weeks and then they finally cut it down to one week and I had to be off. So I went and stayed with Steve and Agnew Findlay, a girl that I was going with then, she was going to take notes for me of the

classes and everything, what was going on, and then what really hurt me so they thought that although I couldn't come to class, that I could come to all the band rehearsals and any performances but the school said no, he can't take part in anything on the campus.

Captain Dryer said it won't be long, a week. So sure enough, the week did pass and we went on back and everything and got back in school and all that is over and I don't know, got to be around with this other girl, Blanche, I believe it was Blanche Franklin, and Agnew kind of got wind of that and she got to thinking about how--
Agnew was who?
Agnew was my girlfriend who was taking all those notes.
Agnew?
Findlay, a girl out of Mobile, Alabama.
Anyway, so I just said altogether, I don't know, what it was is one big affair

that you look forward to in the band, you see, I mean like this ROTC like I was telling you about, they had captains and lieutenants but if you were in the band you couldn't be any captain or lieutenant but they would put you in the category of a warrant officer and then you could go to the officer's ball when it was held there.

So it was coming time for the officer's ball and I was going to take Blanche to the ball, and then, to show you how different things are now, we had--they would have the dance in the gym but you would go to White Hall, that is the largest building, being the girl's dormitory, and you could go in the waiting room and wait until your girl came downstairs and so, we were in there and so I was kind of winking at Agnew after that and the boys knew that she played piano, and so one of the guys,while we were waiting for everybody to come down, Agnew, why don't you play a number on the piano for us, while we're waiting around, and she played,
That's a very unique name for a woman. Agnew?
Yes.
A-G-N-E-W?
Yes. Agnew Findlay.
And so we went on to the dance and of course after the thing we were nothing but school sweethearts, but I went on with Blanche from then on in. She was out of Houston, Texas.

As we went on, as I said, we would go to--one of the reasons why I wanted to be in there, I liked the music and then you see, the band would get to travel to the football games and everything, and so when we went to Mobile--not to Mobile, Montgomery, when they played Alabama State, we went there and then it was over, Erskine Hawkins band would play, and of course Erskine was kind of Freeman guys, and then Steve used to say, well, I got him

coming, and so everything went on averagly. When I finished, still not dreaming that that would be my career, I came back to Sand Springs--that's where my brother was teaching--and so while I was there he said, well, what are you going to do? I said I'm going to find me a job of something. I'll go around Tulsa and see. He said that's good; one thing, don't worry about it, I want you to be some help to me, Captain Dryer told me that I should be proud of you, that you could help me.
He had a large band, the Pythian Lodge, a large organization that they had and they had pythian band.
Your brother?
Yes. They had a pythian band, and of course he taught in high school at Sand Springs, that's a little suburb town.
I went there and then for a while he would go and he would see me going on little trips and sometimes he turn the band over to me,
the marching band, over to me. I liked that.
Did your brother play an instrument?
Yes, he was a trumpet player. Remember, I told you before, Captain Dryer said why in the world did Clarence let you come here without some kind of horn.
That's right; I lost track.

Anyway, I was with this marching band, but I came on over to Tulsa and met some Tuskegee (inaudible), and one of them--two carpenters, they were a lot older than me, they were about my brother's age, and they were doing quite a bit of work, and when I told them I was a Tuskegee grad, they said yeah, and so a guy from the western part of Tulsa was building duplex apartments and he told them that he wanted that wired and so I told him okay and I did the wiring.
He said, have you had it inspected; I said inspected? I said no. He said you have

to be inspected before you can turn the electricity on. He said, I didn't question you because I figured you knew what you were doing, but you have to have a license (inaudible) and he said, now, are you sure it's all right. So I said so far it is (inaudible), but I said it's wired okay and everything.

So he said okay then, I'll get Spot and Tate to have it inspected for you, and have them come out and look it over, and so that was a colored electrical contractor then, Spot and Tate Electric Company. So they came out and looked it over and they said, that's pretty good, you got a little change in the box, but everything else is all right (inaudible), and they asked me how I got the job--they went to school where I came from--so they said, do you want a job and I said sure, and they said you can work for us.
This was?
Spot and Tate Electric Company.
Spot was one man's name and Tate was the other; Spot and Tate Electric.
Before I make a change in the tape, could you still do electrical work, can you still do it?
Well, a little bit.
(Side A of Tape 1 ended at this point. Transcript will continue in accordance with Side B.)
(Side B of Tape 1 begins at this point.)

I began to get around and meet some of the musicians in Tulsa, so I got acquainted with a young man who was working for an oil company, William Ball, and he said he would call me up when he got a gig. I made a few gigs with him and another man I got acquainted with, T.D. Thomas, a piano player, and he had done some work with the blues band, but he didn't have an organization, but we played a few gigs.

Again it came up some number came up and sang her number and sang her number and he would say, my goodness, you should sing too, that would be a lot of help to you, but somehow I couldn't get it in my that I could sing.

So anyway, those two gigs along with my regular job was pretty nice and so as I told you, I was working for this electric company and one day I was making a round, somebody got a trouble call or something, at one of
apartments at Greenwood and Archer, and I heard some music. A little group of high school guys were playing in the hall, in the Royal Annex Hall.
You were on a trouble call for your electric?
Yes.

And so, I just walked in a while and talked to them and said, when do you rehearse and they went on to tell me about their schedule and they said, do you play? And I told them I play a trombone and they said, how come you don't come here and sing with us sometime? And so I said well I will.

I would just like to mention something before--that's just the beginning of my first being around a band, but a very important thing I'd like to say, while I was doing the gig with Ball and the gig with Thomas it was getting around that there was some youngster in town that plays a pretty good trombone. So, Butterbeans and Susie came to town and Eddie
Heyward Sr. was in charge of the band, and he wanted to augment the band. He was going to be in the Dixie Theatre for two weeks and this is on the TOBA*circuit--
There was a Dixie Theatre?
Yes. Butterbeans and Susie.
Eddie Heyward Sr. was the--
Was the bandleader.
The father of--
Of Eddie Heyward, Jr.
Of Begin the begin?
That's it.

So somebody told him--I think the man that ran the theatre--he asked what he wanted, and he said well, I want a trumpet and I would like to have a trombone for this gig in here, and he said there's this younster around here who plays. By coincidence, the theatre was only about a half a block from the
* Theatre Owners Booking Association

electric shop where I was working, and they had told him that he works down there at this electric shop. So he made it his business one morning to come down and talk to me and said that he'd like me to work with him, and I told him yes, I'd be glad to. He said--he was kind of nice--he said, first, do you read? And I said yes, fairly. He said we'd have to have a rehearsal before I could just tell you it's your job. I said okay; when? From the beginning, I don't know why, the bosses were very nice to me and when they found out I was playing, he said well, anytime you want, but your time don't go with you then. I said that's all right.
So I went to rehearsal with Eddie, and the first thing they did was (inaudible) and everybody was just smiling. They were surprised. So they threw out the finale and everybody was grinning--
(inaudible)
I think that you were very young and you did well.
Yes, they were just

tickled to death. Finally--which I learned later from experience--they were all happy over me, but this trumpet player that was sitting next to, I think--I know, because he saw I was reading it to a tee but (inaudible), and he said let's jam a little, and Eddie said, you're the very one who didn't want to rehearse, and here's this man that came here and played the hardest stuff we have in the book, what do you want to bother him for, let him go back to his job, the man has a job. You didn't want to rehearse anyway. So this trumpet player gave a kind of wink to the drummer--I never will forget it--and that was the introduction that this drummer had the same number that they were playing and rolled off and then all of them fell in and of course I caught on, and so (inaudible) said to me, take one and I went on with my trombone and Eddie Heyward turned around and he stuttered-- if you know him or ever met him, because his son

does too, but he stutters very bad and he goes ba-ba-ba-ba-I never seen nobody play that much music and play a damn thing; but I'm going to take you, you got a job. He said I got a son just about your age, you got the foundation, I'm going to make a musician out of you. He said how in the world did you read all that music and can't play nothing. So I said I haven't been doing anything like that. Well, that's all right, I'm going to carry you with me.
Do you remember the number that they were jamming?
I don't remember. Anyway, to tell you the truth, I never did amount to anything as far as jamming.
At improvising.
Yes.
The men, frankly speaking, just relived that whole time (inaudible), and you know what you can do and it's all right, and of course they would allow (inaudible).

It would just tickle him to death and everything, and later on, I met his son, and he told me his dad had told him about me and his son--after I had my big band--he was one of the features at the Apollo Theatre and the Royal Theatre with my band.
The Royal in Baltimore?
Yes, the Royal in Baltimore.
And he had a small combo and at that time, in his band, he had bad boys--Ernie Royal was the trumpet player, wasn't he? What is the saxophone player's name?
Marshal
Marshal Royal was playing with him, was playing with Eddie Heyward Jr.
Yes, I saw them at Shep's Playhouse in Los Angeles during the war.
Yes, he was playing with him.
Later on, before this is over,
I'll show you a picture that Butterbeans and Eddie gave me, autographed, wishing me luck and everything.
So you didn't get the opportunity to back Butterbeans and Susie?
Oh, I worked that whole season.
Oh, did you work with them?
Oh yeah I did, he had me wrapped in but he wanted me to go and travel with him.
He wanted you to go on the road.

Yeah, but when I looked over things, I kind of felt, I got my job here, I've been playing on the side and--you're young, Preston, but you know those vaudeville shows were bad, that's how Basie got stranded here in Oklahoma and Kansas--and I just figured I didn't want to start out doing like that. I saw they were way over me as far
as music but now if they're so much over me and you have to live like that, well I just couldn't see it and I didn't go.

Well anyway, I'm still not with any band and don't have anything else around there, so the next thing that came up, before it became any band time or anything, Jameson-- I don't remember Jameson's first name. They brought him into the theatre just to play for those silent pictures--a piano player. He would play and get little gigs on the side and that's how Butterbeans and Susie were going on when this Jameson came in. He would get some of the musicians--whenever he would get a little gig--to play with him, and one day, I was on a gig and a youngster came up about my age, and he just stopped and looked funny, up and down; he said, is this Ernest Fields? I said yeah, and it was Walter Thomas--yeah, Foots Thomas. He said, what are you doing? I said, I told you I was going to school, I'm an electrician. He said, I'm a carpenter but I

can play a horn, and I said I can too. So he said we got to get together then and I said yeah. It was in the summertime then, and hot and the wiring, crawling up into the attic on the job and he said, man, I think I can get you something better than this. So I said what. He said I was playing with the Missourians, and they have told me that a guy has brought in (inaudible); an entertainer, a vocalist, that is a terrific showman and they have money behind them, and says they're going to call me. He said will you go if I can get you? I said I'll think about it. He said you better do it, because this is going to be something.

So we would play all around and we would run over to Muskogee sometimes and play a gig and he said you sure got to find out about getting this job. So finally, he would play with this Jameson guy, and I would too, and he finally told Jameson--but he was doing carpenter work--he finally gets his call from way up in Missouri, Kansas and told them to
come, which for that day and time, I think they were guaranteed fifty dollars a week and might have had a chance to make more.

So, he goes and he said when I get down there I'll tell them what kind of fellow you are and I think I can get you in when I get there. He asked them first and they told him to wait, we got it arranged for you now.

As soon as he got there, he called back and said come on, they said all right and I told Jameson and he said well, why don't you wait a while and see how long he's going to get that fifty. Then I said well, if they want to, if they offer that, Jameson couldn't believe it, he thought maybe he wasn't getting it or something, he said let's wait and see; I don't want to hold you back, he says, but Fields, you got to figure it out. He says, you got this job on the side and the people like you and they let you off anytime you want and a lot of times you make more than fifty dollars; and this is
going over there, away from home, and expenses. He said you do whatever you want. So I said, I'll tell you the truth, (inaudible). So anyway, he kept on, Walter talking to Mo and I turned it down--
He went with the Missourians?
Yes.
Fifty dollars a week was riches.
I told Walter that I believe I'll stay on where I was.
Walter went on with the Missourians?
Yeah, yeah.
And fifty dollars a week was riches, a lot of money.
Sure was.
Later on, when they changed it from the Missourians, they contacted me again, but at that time I had then started with this

little group, that I told you when I was going on the trouble calls, a bunch of high school boys. I think one young man wasn't in high school, but it was Roy Milton. Roy Milton was drummer and Roy Randall was the leader who is now (inaudible). He was the leader of the bunch and Oscar Warner was in the group, Booker--I'm getting mixed up--but anyway none of them turned out to be well known other than Roy Milton, as far as that group. I went on to play with them.
So we played a while, when Roy Randall, who was the leader, he said let's let him be the leader, he seems to know a little more about music than we do.
Talking about you?
Yes, talking about me. And all the others said yeah, that's okay, they all went for it.
So then that's where I had taken them over. So when Foots called me then about this Cab Calloway, he said it's going to be sensational, you better come on now, because he

said something about we're going east, they won't be trying to get anybody back this way after then and you'll be right in on the ground floor. I told Foots, well, no, I started with these little boys, but it might work up to something, Walt, and I believe I'll stick with it along with my little job for a while yet. So he said okay and went on and I turned that down. So we just played around and we would gig and so finally I got a gig up in--a guy by the name of Lloyd White--I forget how he got in touch with me or something, but the reputation that there's this little band in Tulsa and they'll travel. You see, lots of bands would play and be nice, but with their jobs they couldn't get off, and so that I could leave town. So this Lloyd contacted me and I went up to Hutchin, Kansas, we had three or four dates in that area and Wichita, and played and I met Eddie Nicholson there.
The drummer?
Yes, Eddie Nicholson the drummer. And he said I kind of like your band and everything (inaudible).

So Roy Milton, I had a talk with him and I told Roy, I said Roy, I'm still with you, I says, but I'm going to put you in front of the band, so you know you're all right with me, and so I put him like they called the entertainment. I put Roy Milton up there and I got Eddie Nicholson on drums.
Do you know the approximate date and how you were at that time?
When I came out of school in twenty four, I had just had turned twenty one.
And now you were approximately?
I would say about twenty two, twenty three; something like that.
That would have been around nineteen--
We were still in the
You were twenty three and you were born in 1904?
Yes.
So it would have been around 1927.

Maybe it was; it might have been a little earlier. So anyway, I put him in there and it made a lot of difference as far as the sound when Eddie was playing, because Eddie was a very nice drummer, a very good drummer.
He's a lovable person; I know him very well. The original hip cat.
As I said, I was just tickled over Roy and we would play and were doing pretty good, and a young man came to town--did you ever know a Phil Dorsey?
No, I didn't.
Well, this Phil Dorsey was from Omaha originally, but I guess that is before you got into the business, and he was

hanging around--he came with some group--but he was a musician, but he was some kind of promoter and talked way down deep in his stomach--a very intelligent guy, and he goes, you've got a pretty good band, Fields, and said, I'm going back to Omaha and I don't (inaudible), and he said, I'm going to get you up in that area, but he had good connections around in Kansas. And so, sure enough, he did come and he gave me a call.
Howard White?

No, not Howard White, this Phil Dorsey (Inaudible). At the same time, before then we--they were doing doing this taxi dance, ten cents a dance, and we got to play a few of those and it caught on I go to Ponca (phonetic spelling) City.
Oklahoma?
Yes.
So then a white trombone player came down, Dave Duncan, and he said I like your band, how come somebody else (inaudible). He

said he was down somewhere and wanted to join Jack Teagarden, but he had a small group and so he couldn't hire me and here you are, you're a trombone with a little group, so I guess you say you don't need me, and he said, let me tell you, I can do more than that. He said, I arrange and I can play piano. So I said, you're an arranger and he already was on me that he wanted to do something a little different, not just play, because I had already began to buy stocks--you know, arrangements, but I always like to have different, if we could.

So I said, we could try to see what we could figure out, and he says, okay now, and he gave me his address. I didn't take him right then and he laughed, he said you're just trying to be nice and I said no, I'm going to try and figure out something. I got back into Tulsa and I had a call from Gladewater, Texas, they wanted bands down there, there's this big oil boom in east Texas then and wanted a band in Texas. Now, Gladewater and Longview in not
far from Nacodoches, so I said to some of the boys, I'll have to go down and see where I was born, and we laughed.
Did you have any people left in Nacodoches?
No.
Before you go on, would you like to explain how the taxi dance worked?

What it was is you would go into a place and the guy would tell you that you've got to do so many dances an hour, to figure out the money he's going to make, and it's ten cents a dance. You've got to be on your P's and Q's. If I remember right, I believe no dance could be over three minutes.
Each couple paid ten cents?
Yes and they had the girls, they paid the girls to come and he's selling tickets.
You were were on percentage?
Yes. If they were really going good, they're going to pay you, but a lot of them were on percentage.

So this guy, this job we were going down to Gladewater and Longview to play, and so we're going down there and this guy would give us a salary. I forget what it was, but they'd give us nice money, around ten dollars a man and that was big money. I think the fellow really meant well, but it rained, rained every night and you couldn't get there hardly for the mud, and it just was bad.
Was this a black guy or a white guy?
No, it was a white guy.

It was very fortunate, I started off, I didn't develop the idea of playing all the time of what I wanted to play. I played what the people wanted me to play, and so that made me do a lot of white work also, just as

much as I did, and through the years, that was proven even when I got to recording, and so anyway, this guy got a nickel too, this kind of manager, and I had borrowed money to come down there, I had borrowed some money from my brother, who was teaching, and I borrowed some money from him, I had this job.
Gladewater, Texas?
Yes.
Those were two oil boom towns, and the ballroom was just in between them. I think we lived in Longview.

Yes, the personnel in that band was Luther West, Roy Milton--
Luther West, alto?
Yes.
Roy Milton was the vocalist and we called him the entertainer, and Eddie Nicholson was drums and Cecil Smith was guitar and Roy Walker was trumpet, a young man who at one
What's his name again?
Roy Walker, trumpet player.
He had a brother, Joe Walker, and Joe played with Louie also.
There was somebody else in there besides--oh yeah, Pete Bailey was on tenor. Luther West, alto, Pete Bailey on tenor and Roy Walker trumpet and me on trombone.
What was the nickname you called Luther West?
Spurjeons.
He's dead now?
Yeah, he's dead now.
You called me when he died.
Sure did.
Twenty years now?
Close to it.
He ended as a mailman, wasn't it?
That's it.
Fine alto player.
A very fine alto player.
You know this Ron spoke about him and somebody was telling somebody.
The first time I saw you and met you in 1941 in Denver, what were you playing, the Rainbow Ballroom?
I believe it was.
And I was with Lloyd Hunter's band, my first big band, Spurgeons, Luther West was on alto and I saw you at the Dreamland Ballroom with Spurgeons; excellent player.
Yes.
Go ahead.
This guy, after he didn't do anything, we got a little cash, and
he wrote us a check, because I borrowed this money from my brother, and I sent it right on back to him. Every one of them bounced.
The checks bounced?
Yes. Every one of them bounced.
And so the next day, while we were around there, I got my first taste of really the South.

Pete Bailey just happened to walk in, something had gone wrong at the hotel where we were staying and one of the Texas Rangers officers were questioning some people around there, and Pete Bailey didn't know what was going on and he happened to walk in and this ranger looked around and saw him and he didn't hit him with his billy, but he took his hand and slapped him and practically knocked him down. Pete said what? Nigger, don't interrupt. He said, I'm not interrupting. Well, you didn't know, don't be coming in here when you see that I'm busy.
That was a Texas Ranger?
Yes.

So we went out and there wasn't anything to do, Pete didn't want to go around there anyway and what made it so bad, he went in as a favor for me, his dad ran a pool hall in Tulsa and they had--whatever year that was-- twenty seven or twenty eight--- had a brand new Studebaker and they let Pete have it. His dad had told him, his old man talked kind of slow--I don't know about that car down there, something might even happen.

So sure enough, Pete said we ain't got no money, let's go back, and so all of us felt kind of bad and then I think Eddie Nicholson said, yeah, if that had of been me, he would have had to kill me, a man hitting me for nothing, and so we all got together and decided we were going to go and talk to this man. So he said, my goodness, it's been bad luck, but I'm going to pay you--ask Sugar Lou and Eddie
that's a rock band, at that time, something like Georgia Lee in East Texas, they were very popular.
Suger Lou and Eddie?

Yes. Sugar Lou and Eddie. Both of them sang and they had a five or six piece band and so this guy said, ask him, I don't work no bands and don't pay them, and he did. He somehow got money. He said I can kind of see how you all feel and I said, goodness, we don't have to go through that, and so we came back home to Tulsa and were playing around there.
By the way, where was Sugar Lou--
I think their home was Tyler, Texas.
Was that a brother-sister?
Yeah, I think they were. I'm not positive--yeah, they were brother and sister. They had a very nice group, one of
the best known around there.
They were from Tyler?
Yes, from Tyler, Texas.
I never heard of them; I'm surprised I haven't.

Again, right at that time, T. Holder began to come to. He came on back, but of course, before then, what encouraged me to go for the band, Al Trent, Alphonso Trent would come to Tulsa and I would just stand in front of his band and he had a youngster in there, Lee Hilliard; he played trumpet and alto.
Yeah, Lee Hilliard.
Trumpet and alto. He was younger than me, I think he was even in his teens then, and they had another youngster, Leslie Sheffield--
I worked with him. We went to Canada together in 1943. Leslie died recently in Oklahoma City.
Yeah, in Oklahoma
City.

Alphonso Trent was watching and we came on back to Tulsa and then about that time T. Holder was around. T. Holder was at the Louvre Ballroom and of course T. Holder--I think they were doing the taxi dance in there.
What was it called?
Louvre, L-O-U-V-R-E, I believe.
It's now--they changed the name later on, a dance teacher took it over--Kane, they changed it to Kane's Ballroom.
Downtown?
Yeah, downtown.
Now, T. Holder and Alphonso Trent were two of the great southwest bands.
That's it exactly.
Of course, T. Holder came from Alphonso Trent--he was a trumpet player. Well, I did a special trip in Muskogee to talk with Trent before I came up here. I don't mean Trent--
T. Holder?

T is still living, he's in his eighties. He's not too sharp but he remembers some of that and remembers me and he remembers how they would have these rehearsals and he wouldn't let anybody come in. He would have closed door rehearsals, where they came to the door and they would say Ernie Fields is here, he's got a little band, and he would say, let him in. And then I'd go and rehearse, and I learned an awful lot from him.

I remember one day that he was lecturing to his guys and he told them that I don't want to see what happened last night, and I think somebody says what? He said, so and so is playing a solo and made an error and said it just tickled you to death and everybody went looking around at each other. He said if you are not playing your horn and setting the rhythm for the soloist, if he does anything wrong, you better be grinning and clapping your hand like he played it right. And he said if
you're beyond making mistakes, you got no business in the band, and he said I don't want that to happen anymore. It was a good idea that he was saying that, because all the guys took it in.
Another thing, he--maybe it is good and maybe it is bad, but T would play--I got to be pretty close to him, because Andy Kirk went on to the big time-that was T. Holder that made that band.
I know.

I was right there, and so when he wasn't talking about the gambling what T would do at that time, he had about a twelve piece band which was big money, they were only getting about seven hundred dollars a week, that's less than a hundred dollars apiece, but when they paid T off--Faulkenberg would pay him off--he was married to a woman in Dallas, Texas, he would walk out the back door, get in his car and head for Dalllas and if he won, when he came back they got their money and might get a tip;
What kind of gambling did he do?
Poker, craps, anything; he was just a gambler, and would gamble on all the guys' money.

Finally, Faulkenberg said to me-- another man that encouraged me to get a big band--right at that same time, he said he had a talk with the band. He said you all are getting to be too much of a headache; he said, can anybody run the band? He said I don't have anything against T, but it's too much headache. He said I'm surprised you all are not tired of it. I pay him, he goes to Dallas, half the time he's losing money, you're begging me for money, you owe your hotel bill, you got nothing to eat and everything. He said somebody needs to get somebody for a manager, or somebody else to handle the money.
And so, when T came back that
time, they voted him out. They weren't going to put him out of the band, because they all liked him, but they wanted him to let somebody else handle the money.
The business?
Yes, the business of it and they wanted--he never did lie about the money, but you just weren't going to get what you were supposed to get if he got in that game and lost.
So they voted Kirk to do that and T wouldn't go for it.
Andy Kirk?
Yes.
Andy was playing in the band?
Yes, saxophone and bass. Andy was a bass player too.
I know.
So they made him the leader and so I said if that's what you want, but he was going to be boss. He had guts. He

said I'm going to be boss all the way.
And so, at the same time--I don't know Jack's first name--I mean last name, but there was a piano player named Jack, and I made a special trip to Muskogee and T remembered me coming in (inaudible), but Jack was a very fine piano player and he got sick. John Williams was playing alto and Mary Lou was piano, but Mary Lou then was just kind of going around with the band, and so, when Jack got sick and was ill several weeks, T sent him home just to straighten out and let Mary Lou play while he was gone.
So Mary Lou was playing when this change came, and I was still working--I didn't have to work if I didn't want to in the electric shop, and I got acquainted with all the boys and when that change came around, Kirk came to me and said Ernie, they made me leader and said you know what happened, T's all right, but he just couldn't go on with what he was doing. He said I'm not going to get Jack back, he said Mary Lou is too wonderful, and he said I'd like
Did you loan him the three dollars?
Yeah, and he paid me back too.
You never played with T. Holder?
No.
Nor Andy Kirk?
No.
You just knew them around?
Yeah.
I think I did once a little with T, but not while he was having a band. You see, his home was Muskogee and so what he would do
is he would maybe be gigging and me and Foots and Foots had a brother, Joe Thomas--I don't know if you heard of him.
Oh, certainly.
Well, we would all play together.
A little more about Alphonso Trent.
You probably played for him later in Fort Smith, Arkansas towards the end of his life.
I definitely did.
I did too.
I sure did.
Trent was one of the great bands and at the time that I met you in 1941, Trent was in town too working--wasn't his wife a musician or something?
I don't exactly know.

We're getting a lit-
tle ahead of the story, but I must mention this, well, it may not be exactly ahead of it, but I spoke about this Phil Dorsey.
From Omaha?
Yeah, from Omaha.

And so Dorsey, that all came about after the Gladewater deal, and then Dave Duncan then, something when I came back, my mind told me, now you're trying to build this band, you need an arranger all the time in there. I called Dave Duncan in Ponca City and asked him to come join the band.
This is the white guy?
Yeah, Dave Duncan was a white guy.

So Dave came on and was grinning and so my mother--you see, we had a big house in Tulsa then and so I said I would like for Dave to stay in one of the rooms. And she said what? She said son, what do you think the people are going to say? He can go and stay anywhere. I said mama, I'm not making enough money

for him to go stay anywhere like he can. Well, you know it's all right but what about the neighbors with a white guy staying here. So I said to her, mama, you're talking like they talk now, they always say it's all right, but. And so Dave stayed with us in our home. He had a room there. That's the way we're advertising it, but it's going to be a big thing, you
What year was that?
I would say--because Eddie Nicholson was there--it must have been around 1930, approximately; somewhere along in there. Not over thirty one or two, because it was kind of during the depression.
I think people might not understand, it was revolutionary, for a white guy to be with a black band; that was a big thing.

I told him right then you can say you're the manager or anything and he said I understand, and he was a very fine fellow and a good musician and the only thing after he finally left the band, Spurgeons said, I'll tell you one thing--

Duncan?

Dave Duncan, okay boy, white, but he really had us in good condition and everybody got so that they liked him. So Grant Williams joined the band, and he had been known-- now don't get confused about Fats Waller, but he was a saxophone player, I think he was
originally out of Detroit, known as Fats Walls.
Fats Walls?
Fats Walls; not Fats Waller.
W-A-L-L-S?
Yes.

He was a very fine sax man and this Grant Williams was with him, and of course he got very well known by him being with this band here, and they had played this Louvre Ballroom. If you had ever played in there, that was really the best. Fletcher Henderson did a week at the Louvre.
Is that an integrated ballroom?
No, it wasn't integrated.
All white or all black?
All white.
So this being Grant Williams' home, he decided he's going to stay, and so he joined my band and so the captain at the Tulsa Club--

Bruce Steele was in there, a terrific white band, and when he was leaving and they would pay a band on a week stand. So they had an opening and this head waiter, Johnson--Captain Johnson--the manager said why don't you see how you feel, give them a try, and so this manager of the hotel, he said well, I don't know whether they'll go for it. He said try it anyway. He even told him let him audition, see what you think about him. He said, well you know about it than I do, if you said all right, I'm just wondering how they'll think about it and everything.
Then he told him about this white trombone player, he said I'll give a week in there.
But you couldn't have a mixed band?
Yeah, couldn't have a mixed band.
How big a band did you have now?
I had about seven pieces then; that's all.
So we went on in this Tulsa Club and he came with us a lot and be around but before we left, you know, he sat in--
This was at the Tulsa Club? Now I'm confused.
What?
This was not at the Louvre Ballroom?
No, this was the Tulsa Club. Very exclusive.

And so later on, I didn't know really how much it counted, but they had two firsts--I think about five years later, like they have what happened on this date in such and such a town--and they had it in there, they weren't saying black then, it was colored or negro, for the first time the Tulsa Club used a negro band for a week and the negro band played the Joanne Skelly outgoing party.
Skelly (phonetic spelling) was an

oil millionaire that had come in to Tulsa, the Skelly Oil Company, and so we played his daughter's coming out party. That was all in the news what happened. And like suddenly everybody got history, well not long ago, senior citizen showed me a book that somebody in Tulsa had written, that one of the newspapers put out, and showed the Tulsa of yesterday, and they had it in there about Ernie Fields, the first negro, and they had all the pictures in there, the first negro band that played the Tulsa Club.

And so we were going pretty good and we still hadn't done this battle of the bands yet and so then after Dorsey and that date was coming by, that was my first time then of saying to my bosses, at the electric shop, I don't know if I'm going back to work. So they said, all we can say is we wish you luck and if you want to come back you've got your job.
So I talked to the guys and they said well if you're quitting your job to go, we'll sure go.
Were you married yet?
Yes--no, no, I wasn't married yet. I was still single then. So I went onto Denver--
You went to Denver; now Dorsey was bringing you out there for the battle of the bands?
Yeah, for the battle of the bands. I had one or two little gigs, but the main one was to play at the battle of the bands.
So Roy Melton, when I told him about it, he went and put the little sparklers in so that when the lights show up--
Megaphones?
No microphones.

You got him out of

Yes.

Yeah, From Trenton, New Jersey.

And so, it seemed like it was even all along, and Scotty--I never will forget it--

Herbert Scott, which we had made up--I never did write, but I would give guys notes and tell them. Miff?
Yeah, they called me Miff Mole, you know.

So he said, Miff, play I'll Always Be In Love With You. So I called it and we swung that down and Roy got out there and the people got to whistling and howling and carrying on and that made Billy Stewart angry. He had a little short drummer and Duke had just

At that time then (inaudible), I said I'm going to be like Faulkenberg told me, get your big band, you can do it. And so Eddie Nicholson told me, yeah, yeah, I've been telling you that and so we went on, but after all we did have a little seven piece band, we did all right, but Smiling Billy Stewart had about a ten or twelve--no, I think it was twelve or fourteen--he had a big band, it was a good band, and I never heard of him before, but they were Smiling Billy Stewart and the Sarasota Serenaders.
Where were they from?
Florida. They were out of Florida. They had a terrific band.
So we went on and we got paid, and then Jones-did you ever know Jones the promoter

Where was it held, what ballroom?

It was the ballroom right there on the points, Rosonia. Jones told me, I'll tell you what, Smiling Billy is a long way from Florida, he comes once a year, but he said I'll have you in here a lot of times, and I told him okay. But I told him then, come back again, I think I'll have a different size band, a little larger.

So I went on back then, when we did go back in Tulsa, we played those dates-- what's his name--Dorsey--had several dates and we played around and went back and Spurgeon was still going to school down in Xavier and I never would encourage him to stop school and I think Bostic had Scott around, Earl Bostic, and whenever I couldn't get Spurgeon I'd used
Bostic.
Earl Bostic worked with you?
Yeah, Earl Bostic. And so I still liked Spurgeon better as a band man than lead sax, but boy, I tell you, Earl Bostic blowed more horn, he was just a genius. I felt really close to Bostic.

The band director there, William Jett, in Tulsa High School when it started, he was from Hampton University, Hampton and Tuskegee are very closely related and we got to be kind of buddy-buddy and run around together, and he used to say to me, I'm going to have a good man for you--talking about Bostic--in the high school band--and he gave Bostic a clarinet and his dad was a junk man. Bostic's father?

Yeah. He said my goodness, you're going to be blowing that thing around here, my son ain't going to be. And so from what I understand, the mother cried and everything and she called me and said you're a good friend of Mr. Jett, call him and tell him what happened, but I'll pay him for it.
That was a school clarinet?
Yeah, a school clarinet.
So I told him and he said Ernie, you can tell her she won't have to pay one penny, I'll pay for it. That was the band director.
What was his name?
William Jett.
He said, she and everybody is going to be proud of that boy, the old man just don't know. He and I laughed about it. Here's a junk peddler talking about he don't want his

By the way, did you know that Bostic went to school here in Omaha, at Creighton University?
Yes, he and another young man from there, Sam Abner.
Abney or Abner?
One or the other. He's from Tulsa too. He came here and West, they weren't exactly the same classmates, very close, but West went to Xavier in New Orleans.
By the way, so Luther would play with you just intermittently and go back to school?

By the way, where did he get the name Spurgeon?
I don't know how that nickname came about.

You called me in 1943 and I was working--Johnny Littles and I were working at Sloppy Joe's, to join your band. You called me several times and I joined Basie--I was going to join you and Basie came and took me September 4, 1943.

Anyway, Bostic went on and they were all right and he came out just overnight, just saxophone fine, and then it was Freeman, a Catholic teacher--both of those boys were Catholics--and they went to the public school but they also studied Catholic and this Catholic teacher was music, and he got a little band. Anyway, Spurgeon goes to Xavier and he came back one summer--it was the latter
He also played trombone.

So Spurgeon said he's a fine fellow and nice and clean cut and whatever he says he's going to get, he's going to get. Spurgeon said I wouldn't be going back to play with him if he wasn't, and everything is fine. So she said, I tell you what, I'm going to consent for him to
go because I'm afraid for him, he's about ready to kill somebody.
Who? Rene?
Rene.

Rene was in a little Golden Glove and he went to Biloxi--Spurgeon said his mother told him--and the blacks won and so, the man-- the promoter, they were going to jump on the colored boys and beat them up because they had won and he gets an iceman to slip him into the ice truck, covered up like it was an ice wagon and get the guys back and he had to come back later, somebody to get the cars.
Is that right?
Rene Hall was in that?
Yeah, yeah.

So when he got home, his mother-- he goes downtown and he went downtown and bought him a pistol, so he came back home and his mother said, Rene, what in the world are you doing with that? Mama, I ain't running no more. If this happens again, I'm going to get me one

And she said no, if it got like that, you just got to give it up. So she called up the guy up that had the youngsters and told him that she wasn't going to let Rene go out of town no more, that he could work around there but he wasn't going to go out of town.
So when that came up, she said I think I'll let Rene to go with you and so then Rene did come on to Tulsa then.
While we're talking about Rene, he began to work around and everything, and he was just watching me, and so one day he said to me, I sure don't want to go down South with you,

and I always was a person that would ask questions and I said why, Rene? He said well you're talking to white folk. I said, am I wrong? He said, no you're not wrong, but you've just been around this area, this may be the South, but it's a lot different in the deep South. You're not supposed to be right with them, you've got to be agreeing with what they're doing. And so we just took that in and went on.

I guess it was maybe a couple of years, I didn't get any booking down in the deep South, but he was writing arrangements and everybody was just tickled over it and I said, I sure wish I could play the guitar. He said I'll tell you what, I'll make you a deal, you teach me guitar and where you're always telling me how you want somthing arranged and I'll teach you arrangement--you teach me trombone. And so I said that's a deal, and I guess that I lasted maybe about three months, but Rene would continue on. He said we made that deal and I'm ready for my lesson.

You see, I was booking the band a lot too and he says I know, and I don't want you to give up what you're doing, because you're getting work for us, and he said one reason that I like you is--he said one of the reasons I made up my mind to come with you is I was playing with Walter Pichon, a very fine musician and arranger, but he was too enthused over music. He said, we would have a rehearsal and if a man came up to talk to him about a gig, he would say just a minute. He wouldn't be insulting, but his mind would be on that music; that man might stand there for a half hour to forty five minutes, and he'd get tired and go about his business. And so we had to tell him, that man wanted to give us a gig; oh man, I forgot about that, I was trying to get this arrangement.

And so finally, one time they got a--he saw that the guys were getting kind of tired with the way things were going, they would get a good job and not know when there was another one, so they got a job in some hotel,

in Memphis, a white band, a big white hotel in Memphis, and said Pichon gave one of those little pep talks, he said we got two weeks in there, we'll be in one place for two weeks and we'll have some work, we'll have plenty of work, because I'll be in one place and I can call and get everything lined up.

So they went in there and everything went down just fine and Pichon was so enthused over them going over good and he just forgot about everything and a day or two before it was over, somebody said, Pichon, where do we go from here? I've been so busy, you've all been doing such a good job, I just wanted to keep you on your feet, but we're going back home and we'll get something.
He didn't have any gigs?
He didn't have nothing in the world.
Where did they--
They were out in New
Orleans.
Pichon?
Walter Pichon.
Do you remember how to spell it?

No, but I think I have a picture that he gave me. He's passed now but he was a very fine arranger and we had that arrangement and Rene had him send an arrangement to me after then and we had one that as time changed that never did get old and after Ernie got up big--yeah, my son--he said, dad, there's one thing that I would like to have and that's the arrangement of Stardust that you all used to do, and I lost my whole repetoire. But Pichon was a very fine arranger.
But as I said, when Rene saw how I did things, that's why he (Inaudible), but he would still make me get in his lesson, (inaudible).
They would play a little poker and they would have a session (inaudible), so the

boys would go in another room and win or lose, he'd come on in the room and early that morning, if we didn't have to leave, he'd grab that trombone and somebody would hit on the wall, god damn, cut out that noise and they always said, the folks gonna run us niggers out of here. Man let us get some rest, we have to leave at two. He said I don't care. Man, you know we're in here gambling. He'd say, gambling may be your business, I was in there too, but I got my rest and I'm going to practice.
Would he use your horn?
Yes.
Did he have a horn?
He went and bought a horn after a while. He went and bought his own.

And then, when he left my band, he got a gig with Earl Hines as a second bone man; they never did go for all that guitar, you know; Kirk did, but Hines or Basie never did go for all that guitar, and that's what he was playing.

Yeah, that's what he played.

If I had of gone on like he did, I would been on there, but we used to laugh about it then. A lot of guys would leave the band and wouldn't be tight but we were just as tight with him going as we were before.
And he became your very best friend?
Yes, very best. That's what junior was saying, Rene Hall and Roy Melton, anytime you say anything to anybody to them, they would say something about that they worked with Ernie Fields.

You were playing at the Tulsa Club--
And also this going
The coming out party for Skelly?
Yeah, Joanne Skelly. Her going out party. We were kind of on our way---as I said I had given up my job.
You quit the electric job?

Yeah. We had Rene Hall and we began to add a piece or two and I got a young man out of Wichita, Kansas, Delma Willis and Bob Graham on tenor and a fellow came, H.E. How would you travel?

We had two cars and carried the instruments on top of the car. That finally one time got us into trouble. New Mexico had a law that if you were doing commercial work, you had to have a commercial license--
Colorado too.

Sure enough. I'll never forget, Herbert Scott, this fellow that I told you we got from Bessie Smith, he was just so elated that he was a musician, of his job and the band and he was just going to let everybody know what his job is, so we stopped at the port of entry once and this guy went in--I think Scotty--I didn't go, I sent Scotty or somebody told me I better go on in, Scotty was so long and the man looked out and said, what's all that on top of the car, (inaudible). They guy just let him talk. We'll be playing so and so and so and so, and so he said you're going to have to buy a license. So they got me then and I went out and said

How much was the permit; do you remember?
It was very little, it was big money then though. I think it was about twenty five dollars. But if they made us buy a license for that commercial thing it would have been a hundred dollars.
I had to pay ten dollars to go into Colorado, with my bus.
See we haven't gotten to the bus yet. So we made that trip and came back in--I'm trying to think who was on my first trip

Salva had that little fingering that Count finally perfected and Salva's brother--I'm telling you the truth--
Ron mentioned him in his letter? I don't recall.
Yeah, yeah.
Salva?
Salva Sanders.

Anyway, when the news came in to Tulsa, with the group, when these road guys would go in front and book the band, and Salva came in, I believe, with the Southern Serenaders, but he was originally from (inaudible), Oklahoma and had gone to school out in Langston, university, but had left town and joined the Southern Serenaders, but he came in and then

So then I jumped on Frenchie, the saxophone player and Frenchie said yeah, I don't want to go out anymore depending on a whiskey head. The piano player with the group--I forget what they called him--was--the star was the piano player, and this booker had the guys in some theater, he got them to use this band and they had played good in Muskogee and they came to Tulsa in a theater there and booked them and when the lights went on, this cat fell off the stool--the piano player. I don't remember what his name was.

Anyway, he told the booker, I've had it, I just can't put my job up against a whiskey head, I'm going; that's the man that you're featuring, you don't know what condition he's going to be in; so he left.

So I took Salva Sanders then in the band. Another band that came in there was the Texas Rangers and a youngster, Pee Wee Wiley was the vocalist there, he had a voice, he could sing. See, Roy then, when this came up, things had got pretty tough around and somebody, I think it was a drummer, Samson Pratt (phonetic spelling), Samson never did drum with me, but he was around at gigs and everything, and somebody contacted Samson-- let's go to California. Roy had a car--he had made a little money and had married a girl in Tulsa that had this average job and was doing pretty good and he had a car, and he told the boys that we'll just pay for the gas and we'll go out to California and I believe we'll do better than we're doing now.
What three left?
That was Walker, and Roy--
Roy Milton.
Milton, and this Walker and Samson Pratt that wasn't a member of the band.

So when Roy left, I had to hustle a vocalist and so then that's when I got Pee Wee Wiley. It was a coincidence that at that same time the Texas Rangers were in town and so, Salva Sanders had worked with them also and so then he told Wiley, you know I left them and went to the Southern Serenaders, but this Ernie Fields band is a better place than that, you better come on in now because he needs a vocalist. And so I got Pee Wee Wiley.
Now as far as Pee Wee Wiley, he

wasn't anything particularly bad, but you never would dream that he developed to what he is doing now. He's a minister. Then he was nothing but devilment, but he could sing and he could holler and he finally woke up.

He left later--not with that bunch, but he left later for California, and went to California and then years later when I went there he had taken me out to dinner and had me-- he wasn't pastor, but a very good church out there in Watts, he was the assistant pastor.
Pee Wee Wiley?
Pee Wee Wiley.
He's Reverend Wiley now.
Yeah, he's Reverend Wiley now.

And so, anyway, then we got to kind of move on, there I was, it looked like I always had those good vocalists, and at that time that was what was setting the band then. Now, T. Holder had Billy Maxted and I would talk to T and I don't know anybody this and

that, and so finally Don Albert came to Tulsa and Melvin Moore was with him, and I had been going wild over Roy and Pee Wee, but now this is it. And so, he told me, I don't know he said, I told my dad I was going to finish high school anyway and I think he said next year I'm going back to school, I just got one year.

Oklahoma City.

So then we got talking and he said Oklahoma City is right close, I could still make a few gigs with you, but soon as I finish, he says, I'll join the group but I'm going to finish high school. He said I promised dad that. So I said, well, I can't hardly talk against that and I'd say well, I guess you're thinking right, because I didn't have at that time--later on I had a band as good as Don Albert; Don Albert had one hell of a band, and so sure enough, never left Don and went on back then and I just picked up somebody and we made

When school was out (inaudible).

Yes.

I saw Melvin at the Apollo with you.

I did.
That was years later,

Willard Alexander.

--that he was going to pull out from William Morris as soon as his contract was out, and he was trying to deal some bands to go along. Russell Moore, Big Chief?
Big Chief; yeah.
Indian from Omaha.
Yeah.

Anyway, I told the guys I'd see

tell you what, you went over really good down
in Philly and if you know you're going to go

but he said I think he can throw you a couple

He said, have you got any con-

He said maybe I can get you one stop between

Rozelle Claxton.

How were you travelling, did you have a bus by then?
Yeah, I had a bus then.
Where did you get the bus?
Well, you see, we
just jumped into this Melvin Moore that I was telling you about, but I'm going to come up with when we got the bus later on.
So anyway, he said I wish I had your shotgun and some birdshot, I'd shoot him; a man who couldn't go to New York City and meets us out here ain't got no brain; what kind of brain does that man got?

Well, you know, you told me a story earlier, and I'd like--now I think would be the appropriate time, how Willard and John Hammond got in touch with you. You see we talked about that but it's not on the tape.
Okay.

Well, Hammond was still trying to find something else
