And he told him no. He said, is that a band here? He said no but he has a mighty fine band. So he said, where is he? He said he's an Oklahoma band, I think his headquarters are Tulsa, Oklahoma. He just comes in here and plays now and then.

So Hammond got to talking around and of course Yardbird and all the guys in jazz that knew about the Ernie Fields band because I had outstanding men, Luther West and all, they hung out together and all the bands and they would tell him that he's in Tulsa, Oklahoma. So Hammond comes to Tulsa.
He went to the Club Lido, a club in Tulsa and he got in touch with one of the waiters and wanted to know if he knew Ernie Fields and they told him yes, they knew Ernie,

So he said, how could I get a hold of him. He said, well, he has a telephone. So Hammond said would you mind calling him and he said yes and went and called me and I wasn't in, I was out on a gig that night. I remember that week and I was in a little hick town around. So he came back and told Hammond that I wasn't in, that I was playing that night. So Hammond told him again, go call and give him my room number, I'm in the May Hotel and tell him to call me when he gets up tomorrow morning.

So he came back and called my wife and told her to tell me and gave her his room number and the May Hotel telephone number and told her to tell me to call him. So she said okay, but John Hammond didn't mean any more to her than it meant to this waiter at that time. So when the waiter goes back to Hammond, Hammond thanked him and gave him a five dollar bill and he said I don't have the change; he said that's yours. So he comes back to the telephone a third time and he called my wife that third
time and said, Mrs. Fields, I don't know who that is, but you tell Ernie to be sure and contact that me, he apparently is somebody mighty big, he just gave me five dollars for spending a dime.
Five dollars was a fortune then.
That was 1939.
When I got the news, my wife handed me the note, and I woke up, I said what is this and she explained what it was and I don't know if I slept anymore that morning; John Hammond wanted to talk to me.

Of course I knew who he was and everything and so about ten o'clock I called John Hammond. So he says, I thought you worked last night; I told him I did. You're up already? I said yes, I'm up, you said you wanted to talk to me. He said yes, but I thought you'd be getting your rest, I thought you'd call about twelve or one o'clock, and so he explained himself and he said he wanted to catch the group,

could you arrange for me? I said sure. So I called the boys and everything and they hadn't gotten up, I was glad I started early because they hadn't moved out. So I told them and they were all enthused and we went to the Crystal Palace.

One of the co-owners of the Crystal Palace was my ex-boss when I was working in the electric shop, Walter Tate; he was co-owner of the Crystal Palace and I wanted to know if I could get it and he said you know very well you can; he laughed.

So we were on time, whatever time he said, three or four o'clock, and Hammond came down. We set up and played several numbers and just from the first number you could just see he was all smiles; then he would say play me a different type and we would play that; and he was just all smiles. He said, I'll tell you what, the band is terrific, but I'm not a musician but I do know what's good and what I like. If Willard Alexander, who is head of
the band department of the William Morris Agency, if he thinks half as much of you as I do, he'll take us to New York on a tour and I'll get him to sign you up.

So I told him okay and he said when can he come and hear you and I said well, I'll check my itinerary. Well I knew right then several things, but I didn't want him to come to some little hick town where I was the night he asked about me, so I began to try to think of some town where we might have a decent crowd.

So I had a date about two weeks from then in Wichita, Kansas and so I called Hammond at his hotel and I told him that I'd be in Wichita, Kansas on such and such a date and he said well, I'll see how Willard's schedule is and I'll call you back. So after he called Alexander he called me back and said we'll be there, we'll be in Wichita, Kansas and what hall and I gave him the name of the hall and I gave him the address and he said we'll see you.

So we went on and I don't know if I even heard from him--I might have heard from him one time perhaps before then, but all of them wondered, he was so excited about the band, just wondered, was that Hammond. So Melvin Moore,--he just flipped over Melvin-- and Melvin was a younger man than me but it looked like he wasn't excited as I was, he just wondered too if that was Hammond. So he finally said to me, do you think that was Hammond; I said yeah, why not? He said I just don't believe that was John Hammond, John Hammond is a millionaire. I said I know that too, he's one of the things that practically made Benny Goodman, that's his brother in law, spent that money on him. He said, did you look at that (inaudible).
He had a hole in his pants?
Yeah, yeah.
So I said no, I didn't pay any attention; he said I hope so, but I just don't
believe that was John Hammond. So I said, let us all hope it was.

So anyway I heard from him perhaps one time, but that night we went on to Wichita and set up and all and we were in the back end, the bandstand was in the back of the hall, and so we kicked off right on time and fortunately we had a pretty nice dance. Some of the dances wouldn't be good, but we came in real quick and we played it and nobody saw no John Hammond around or Willard Alexander either. So Melvin asked again, he was more concerned than anybody because he said it wasn't John Hammond. So he says, where's your buddy John Hammond? I said I don't know Mel. Well I told you I thought that was just some cat fooling you. So I said I don't know. We had didn't have an intermission.

We played on and at intermission-- it was during those days, you see Preston, I know that is a little before you were in the business, but after all they had seats all around the wall but they didn't have tables like

everybody had, in the middle there. They really came there to dance and they would sit down for a little while around the wall. So when we had intermission, the people would get to the side and sit down and the floor was open then and we looked there and there walked Alexander and Hammond.
Wow.

They came on up and so naturally I went to greet them and Hammond introduced (inaudible). So I asked him, how long have you been here? Oh, we've been here while you were playing a couple of numbers. I told the people at the door I was expecting you and they welcomed us in and we just took a seat back there.

Hammond was like a little kid, practically, he just said--he said, Alexander just wanted to just see how you were going to work your program and you sure had a nice program and everything. He was just tickled.
He talked around and looked us

over and everything and he asked me if I had anybody in the band who can't be fired? And I said no, but why do you ask that. He said, well, you know, a lot of you bands are doing all right but you can always use improvement. The next thing was, are you signed up with anybody? I said no. He said I just can't understand how somebody hasn't signed a band like you. He said, what I was thinking is I'll go and sign you, then somebody that signed a contract two years ago or something and hadn't done anything would come up and say that's my property. Then the next thing about it, you're clean, so you're at least living decent, but you're not making any money, and says, I don't like to get into something, if you have to make a change and you say now this man stuck with me when I wasn't doing anything and I can't feel that I should let him go. He said I don't like to get into those kinds of things. So I said, do you think somebody needs to be changed? He said no; I tell you one

thing though, I like the group, but Joe Jones kind of had me spoiled. He said when he dropped into New York way, he was kicking that Count Basie band, he says, we just hadn't had any drummers kicking no band like that unless it was Chick Webb that just kicked (inaudible).
And the drummer was?
Clarence Dickson; he was my drummer then.
I knew him very well.
So he was telling me nice, but I was just saying--
He was rather light, he's not as dynamic as Joe Jones.
No; that's it.

Then he said I don't know why the leaders a lot of times just think you shouldn't change; (inaudible). I finally broke the ice and he didn't know it, of getting negro bands into the hotels. So Count had an opening in Philadelphia, a hotel--I don't recall the name--
I think it was the
Pittsburgh.

Yeah. So I went over to catch him and he said he was going to be at his opening. So when I looked up, Joe Keyes wasn't there. And I said to Count, where's Joe? He just had too much, I just couldn't bring him on the bandstand and mess us up drunk, I wouldn't do that. I told him, I said Count, how come you don't get (inaudible). Count said don't you know, that's one of the best first trumpet men in the business? I said he sure is, but you're playing tonight without him. He said you need somebody that you know what you're going to have; he may not be the best but you want to know what you have when you're going and Count kind of smiled, and he said I don't like anybody to think anybody is indispensible, and the main thing is somebody you know what you have. But he said the band sounds all right and he said I'd like to sign you up and I have a contract here now and he had two copies. I went to kind

read it and he said, you don't have to look over it now. He said read it by yourself, with the men and everything and if you want to sign it, keep one copy and send me the other. He said I'd like to bring you into New York, I think I can do something for you. Hammond's a recorder, he's over Columbia and if he doesn't record you with Columbia, he will record you on a subsidiary.
On their label.
Yeah, but Hammond records you, and so Hammond told me, yeah, I'll record you when you get there.

And so, that's the way we left. So I talked it over with the guys, did they want to go, and all of them were--they were just tickled to death. Hobart Banks said I don't know, I'll let you know; so I said what is wrong? Did you say that was five years? I said yeah. He said, I don't know if I can be gone from my old lady for five years, so I said (inaudible).
He thought the wife was going to stay back in Tulsa for the whole five years?

Yeah. So I said I don't know and so the rest of the guys said yeah and Hobart said I'll let you know. So anyway, we went on and the next few days we had another gig, I said I'm going to send this contract back to Alexander and I wanted to know what you think, Hobart; no, Fish, I'm not going. He went on to tell me about how old his little boy was and I just hate to leave there and the old lady and all, I just don't think I'll make it. So I said okay but I'm not turning it down. He said I don't blame you--
This is Hobart Banks?
Yeah, Hobart Banks. So I went and called Kansas City, called the union, and wanted to know if there was anybody they could recommend, you know, a piano player, and you know I always dwelled on

that reading, and they said yes, there's one young man, if he's interested, Rozelle Claxton, he'll play anything you want and he's a nice arranger. So I got his number and I called Rozelle, and he accepted. He said you're going to New York? I said yeah, and he said what are you paying? I said Rozelle, we don't work for anything less than scale around here, but I don't know what it's going to be there, I don't know what kind of gigs they're going to put me on, but you ask anybody about my reputation and you'll get the benefit of the doubt if we get into the money. He said just so I'm getting out of this area, I'm with you. I told him to come right on.

So then I said I will wait and see when exactly we're going to leave and I'll let my man work on, because he's been very fair with me--Hobart--I said when I get some idea of when we would leave, I'll get you in time, a couple of weeks before we're going. So I began to get the trade magazines, this and that and
so on, a cross between the Duke and the Count, Ernie Fields that he discovered in there.
So everybody was smiling and everything and there was this Amos Woodruff who I just loved as a musician and everything but that was the only member in the band that read slow--
What did he play?
Trumpet.

A terrific soloist; when he played a solo he never did break the tone. It was just as beautiful as he was playing a sweet solo. If you knew anything about Harold Baker or Louie, that's the kind of style that he played, and he read so slow and you'd have to wait and drill and drill.
Who was first in the band?
Jeff Carrington, a young man out of San Antonio, Texas, out of Texas University--what was that black school, not the University of Texas--
Southern University?
Southern is in New Orleans, isn't it? I mean Louisiana.
You're talking about the one in Houston?
Yeah. Jeff hadn't finished college, but he was from there--
Texas Southern.
Yeah. We'd switch between he and Edwin Milton.
I had two brothers, I had twins in the band, Edwin Milton, a trumpet and Edward on trombone.
Edwin would be on first or either Jeff between and Amos would play second or third all the time.
So anyway--
Amos Woodruff?
Woodruff.
He could catch on? He
Oh, yes, he could follow it very good.
He read slow?
Yes. So anyway, the guys would hum and hum, we finally got a break, are you going to carry Amos up there and embarass us?
To New York?
Yeah, to New York and everything.
The Big Apple?

Yeah, the Big Apple. (Inaudible) Ernie finally got a break, the man that's got Count Basie is carrying Ernie to New York, and he's going to embarass us like that and at first I didn't pay any attention to it, then I began to think about what Alexander had told me; anybody can't be fired and maybe these guys and I got a little ego myself, well maybe I better let them know right quick who's boss and I've been drilling

(inaudible) and here you got a man you know can't read and you're going to carry him along with you. So anyway I got to talking to my arranger, Rene Hall,--Edward Milton did some, but Rene was Rene was one that was the hardest; that's the only run-in I would have. I wasn't an arranger but I used to raise the devil with Rene about so many notes that didn't mean anything in his arrangements.
Over arranged?
Yeah.

And so he told me, he said, I'll tell you what, I don't think any of your arrangements arrange as hard as me, but Amos finally gets it and when he gets it he's got it, you know, and I think you shouldn't worry about that. I was talking to Harry Garnett, there wasn't anybody there in Tulsa that I knew that I could get, or in the area, and Harry Garnett, he was one that played, I found out later, why Alexander liked the band so, he was on the style of Herschel Evans, at that time,

and Bud Douglas, another tenor man was something like Pres, and so they just knocked him out. So anyway, he said I know a man in Chicago I can get, play anything you have in your book--that's Harry Garnett--but I don't know if he would fit like Amos; Amos sure fit this band good. And I finally decided I better give him his notice while I got time. So I gave Amos the notice and of course he was going around like he lost his mother or something; all the rest of the band just grinning and this young man came in and just like Harry Garnett said, he just put the book down--
What was his name?
I forget what his name was, because he was there such a little time.
So I was in Tyler, Texas and we played one date there and since we weren't travelling, we were having rehearsal while we were in there, and one of the guys said, what have
you heard from Alexander and I said (inaudible) and I said I believe I better give Alexander a buzz.
So I called Alexander from Tyler, Texas and I said, haven't heard from you in a good while, when do you think you're going to get us going and he said well, I think (inaudible)--
I played there with Basie, several times.

I just wanted to get things straight and he said you got nothing to worry about, go ahead and rehearse; the band is good, but there's always room for improvement. I said yes, I'm rehearsing everyday if I'm not travelling and I said I even made a change in the band. He said made a change in the band? I said yes, I let Amos Woodruff go, he read so bad and everything and he said I don't know anything about anybody's name in the band, but Fields, I have a very good picture of your group, what did Amos play? I said heavy set
dark trumpet player, sat in the middle. The man almost jumped through the telephone--

--John Hammond wanted, they wanted that feeling, that southwest Texas and Oklahoma feel. They could get readers, guys who could read music and the fancy New York type musicians by the thousands, but that natural, gutsy, soulful feel of the Texas and Oklahoma bands is what he wanted.

That's what I found out, and so anyway, I hired Amos back, put him in there and we left for New York and when we got in we did a couple of sessions and no trouble whatsoever with Amos, and one of the numbers where Amos did solo, he was responsible for the T Town Blues being as big a hit as it was, and if it had really been pushed, I think it would have been a national hit. Amos, frankly, did all of the solo work that we did on all the records; Amos did all the solo work. And if we have a chance before we send them in, see what you think about them.

When I got to New York, another-- now he said how much he thought of him but I didn't know he thought as much of him as he did, was Hobart Banks, the piano player. We got there and Hammond said, where's Hobart? I said Hobart wouldn't come. He said, if you would have brought Hobart, you and Hobart both would have been the happiest two men, nobody could have been any happier. So I said what's up. He said I was going to let Hobart have Benny Goodman-- let Benny Goodman have Hobart, and I said, let him go to Benny Goodman? I said, what are you doing, I'm going to come here and you're going to break up my band. He said you're up here and Hobart's not here and you still have a band; he said we're sending Ernie Fields band, not Hobart Banks. He said I told Benny about Hobart but I also told him, Ernie, that you had a contract on him, he belonged to you and I'm quite sure if he paid you enough that you'd let him have him. He told me see what I wanted, but he would guarantee that he'd give me at least five
He'd give you five thousand dollars?
Yeah.
To give him Hobart?
Yeah.
Benny Goodman?
Yeah.

I said I am sure, and he said that's what I had in mind, because I wanted him to take Teddy Wilson's place. I said I'd sure hate it, and he said Rozelle Claxton is all right and that's what I said, we're sending your band and you're talking how I might have done that but if you were in a new area and didn't know anything, I would have gotten a piano player for you; He said, I wouldn't dare do like what you were talking about, but I was thinking that as a bandleader you need money all the time, and he said that I said to myself, that would be a good capital start for you right there, and so, we all laughed and wished that

Hobart would have been there then. But to show you how he did think about Hobart, you see we're talking about 1939, well whatever date World War II was going on, Hammond was inducted and he did his boot training in Oklahoma, Camp Gruber, right out from Muskogee, which is not far from Tulsa. His mind was still on Hobart, trying to give Hobart a chance so he thought. He grabbed Hobart again and sent Hobart to Cafe Society in New York City, but Hobart just didn't have it as a singer. I'm like Hammond, I think Hobart would have been sensational in the Benny Goodman quartet--
Or in your band.
Or in my band.
But as a singer, he just didn't have it, and I think he had a two week contract and worked him for one week, paid him for two and then sent him back home.
Where's Hobart?
Hobart's passed now.
Hobart worked with me almost until
his death, but he just missed that big deal of going east there where it would have been a break in his life.
Cover the period--how did you go to New York?

I went to New York--had a bus. I didn't buy it just for that trip. Just a little before then, well as I said, we were doing fairly well, we weren't in the money, but I bought a brand new--which was the cheapest bus you could get--like the school bus, but I painted it. I bought it brand new and painted it blue and white so then we had no trouble for a long time.

But before that time, before that bus, it was really comical. We were travelling in those cars and Jack Crawford, white band, had a bus that looked like the old stagecoaches, like something on top, like a caboose, and I'd been kind of working around and trying to get a bus and the Chevy Company, they had ordered a brand new bus for Jack Crawford and I went in

and had been talking around with him, so when Jack got this, some salesman called me, Fields, I have a good bus here, we'll make you a good deal on it, a used bus, and I went and saw it. I went with a few of the boys and we said, this is ridiculous to go down the road in. So we got to thinking it would be better than the car, than piling in the car. So, we got the bus, it was so cheap that I paid cash for the bus; it was the used bus that Jack Crawford was turning in. I don't know if I ever saw anything that looked as funny as that thing; so much that one of the guys, I think it was Brant Thompson, a guy who ran a drugstore, he was crazy about us, he would put on something like he was an indian and say, the stagecoach is coming in, let's rob it and they would all come out like that when we would drive up to let the boys off at the hotel. That's how funny it looked.
Anyway, we drove around for about a season, I guess, and one time, we were coming-- some of the boys would drive and I would drive

sometimes, in Henryetta, Oklahoma, a little town--I never did see this town--I mean, this sign--but they tell me at one time they had a sign up there, Nigger, read and run, if you can't read, run anyhow. I never did see that, but they told me some of them got together and they did move that sign, but no negroes or nothing were in this little town. But we would play other areas and we would come through there.

So one night we played somewhere and was coming through Henryetta and whoever the bus driver was, they let me have it to drive and they were resting up. Some drunk was in the middle of the street, in a car, and I was halfway asleep driving and I went right into the back of them and they had five gallons of whiskey and when I hit them, they didn't know what in the world had happen; they jumped out and ran. So the noise, the police came out and what in the world happened there? I said they were in the middle of the street, I couldn't see them,

what are they doing in the middle of the street there? And of course the officer, you're exactly right, and look here, they're moonshining too. We'll get them and don't you all worry, but I believe it messed up your radiator there, and then they just got to be as nice as they could. They said, we're going to get those guys, they're parked out here in the middle of the street and these guys ran into them and messed their car up. So they were looking after the guys because the whole thing was, they shouldn't have been parked where they were, but I ran into them because I was sleeping.

I'll never forget when the policeman first came up, Salva Sanders was still living then, and he said, go out and say something, don't wait until they say something to you, get out and tell them something, and so I got right out like I knew that they were in the wrong and of course they got right in my corner when they looked in there and saw all that corn whiskey. They said we've been after them anyway, we'll

get them. Then I think I called someone and got someone to put the bus in the garage; this town is only about forty eight miles from Tulsa, maybe fifty, and to show you how things are, (inaudible) black and white live there, but they don't give a darn about Henryetta, but that was the reputation that Henryetta had, that no blacks at all. But they were in our corner, nothing went on, we went back and got my bus fixed and came on in.

We made one little tour with that bus, a very good tour, and did so good and then the band loaned me money to buy this new school bus and I had it painted right then. So we were on time as far as that.
You went to New York in that in 1939?
Yeah, it wasn't too old then; that was the bus that I went in there on.
I always remember the
bus you had in Denver, it was a gorgeous little bus, blue.
Yeah, that might have been it, but later on--
(Inaudible).

Further on, there's always been the comments that the Texas and Oklahoma south-west bands had a distinctive or characteristic sound, especially the tenor players. Do you remember any of the guys like Bridges or John Hardy?
Yeah, John Hardy.

I asked this promoter where's this garage that you said was open all night and he directed us on to the garage, but instead of being a garage, it was nothing but an all night service station. It began to sleet a little, it was then early winter and while we were there, Melvin, who was very popular and was known as much as me because he was on the front line and such a fine vocalist and personality that everybody just took to him, and some of his fans came by and he was outside and they said, are you still here Melvin, and he said yes. So two young men got out of their car and said, what's the trouble? He pointed at the wheel on the bus and I showed them that there were only two lugs on and we just can't make it. So he asked me where we were going and I said we were going to try to make it into Enid, Oklahoma, which was around about seventy-five miles from there and he said you sure can't

go like that in this weather like it is and the wheel will be off. So he said wait a minute; he talked to the service station man and there was nothing he could do, there was no mechanic and that it would be morning before he could do anything. This was around 2:00 A.M. then.

So he got on the telephone and called his dad and it so happened his father had a truck line, a lot of trucks throughout that area and he had a mechanic that worked exclusively for him and so he told his dad that this band was here and the lugs were coming off and to call his mechanic to come fix it. His dad answered--I don't know his exact words--but in other words you can't get any parts this time of night or so on and so forth. So he answered and they had quite a conversation and he said dad, if it was your truck you'd get parts and that's what you're paying him for, to get up and work for you any time of night. And he let his dad know, he said, they're not asking you to do anything for nothing, just order your

mechanic out and they'll pay whatever he charges and from one thing to another he finally decided and persuaded his dad and his dad said can they make it down to my garage, to our house and we told him yes, we thought we could go that far.

So we crept on down to his house and he called--his dad called for the parts and got the parts when he saw what we needed to open up and get what was necessary, and when it was through, he looked around and said, this is the happiest moment of my life.
Who said that?

The young man that had his dad fix it. I asked him what did he mean and he said well, as you see my dad's all right, but there's no negroes around this area at all and they had their own idea and naturally I was raised around them and I thought the same way, and I'm going to school now at the University of Wichita, he was taking agriculture, that's a big wheat area, and he was going for what everybody was doing there, and so he says
the first project they sent him out on, they sent a negro--
With him?

To work with him. And he just went swelling up then but he didn't say anything and finally he and this negro got acquainted, were good friends and he said I wouldn't have passed that first semester if it hadn't been for this negro, and when I came back home I told my people, you all are so wrong about colored people, you just don't know them and haven't been around them, they're just like anybody else, some are good and some are bad, just like anybody else. But to think that I could do something for you just makes me so happy.

Naturally we were headed on our way then to Enid, where we were going and as he was saying, it started sleeting and it got pretty cold the further we got on, so when we got into Enid a little before day, I reckon around about four o'clock or something like that,

or five, everybody was asleep and we asked a policeman--we finally ran into a policeman and we asked him where was a colored hotel, and of course he said he didn't know, he didn't know if they had any, but they had a colored policeman here. He said go down in that area and he explained just where to go, he said his name was Tom, he can explain to you where to go and where you can get lodging.

So we found Tom and he was the only black policeman, just a little token, so when we found him and asked him where there was a rooming house, he said we don't have that here and he went on and talked, he heard of the band and you all are going to play here tonight; we told him yes. So he said we have several negroes that have big homes and said they take in roomers and you could do that but we can't wake them up this time of morning, and he got to thinking, he said I'll tell you what, I can take you on to the jail and sleep on the bunk there and get up and have free donuts and coffee
when you get up; why not do that? He said I'll find you some rooms and everybody kind of looked at each other.

Rene Hall, a young man there, we always roomed together, said are you going; I said yeah, because most of you were sleeping when we were getting the bus fixed and I said I was up then and I want to lay down. So he said I'm going too.

So we two went on and the others said it's okay to run this bus now to keep warm? I said sure, go ahead and run it, and the others decided to sleep in the bus rather than go in the jail. They just didn't want the name that they were in jail, but I went on and when I woke up we got our donuts and coffee.
Enid, Oklahoma?
Yeah, Enid, Oklahoma.
So that was my first and only time in jail, but I certainly enjoyed that morning.
So when we got up we asked about a negro cafe or anything and they didn't even

have that, one little sandwich place or something, but it ain't open until late, but they had one little place, a white restaurant, that had a deal right next to the kitchen, an annex to the kitchen, where he would serve negroes, and so they explained to us where that was.

So we went there and had breakfast and by that time it was around ten or eleven o'clock and it was time for this policeman to get off but before he got off he got us all lined up where we could stay, you know, went around to the different homes.

During that time I got acquainted with a young man, Dewey Goosby--incidentally, he was one of the promoters that would bring us in there and we played that night, the band went over nice and I played for Dewey several times and I was always--even as a kid--liked to hunt and fish, and I got acquainted with him how it was that there were quail around that area. So he said well, Ernie if you're back here for the next date, come on over and you
come in front and we'll go hunting that night. Well Dewey and I got to be pretty tight and I was always glad to play that area, because quail was very plentiful.
In what area was this?
The western part of Oklahoma.
And approximately what year are we talking about?
I would say we were talking about 1936.
This is when you had the incident in Enid, Oklahoma?
Yeah, around 1936 or seven.

So anyway, as I said we played there several times, but then years passed and went on and we didn't hear anything about Enid because I just happened not to be in that area, but during World War II, a lot of the okies migrated to the coast, and Dewey happened to go into the shipyard of Portland.
Portland, Oregon?

Yeah, Portland, Oregon, and of course I didn't know anything, I forgot about Dewey, and I was touring the west coast, the northwest, and Pops McElroy, who brought names in, he'd have Lunceford, Duke and all, but anyway, an area booker I got connected with, and they set a tour for me through there.
McElroy's Ballroom?
Yeah.
I played it with Count Basie, Lucky Millinder.
Yeah, he used to play all the big ones. Pops McElroy.
His son later took it over, after Pop.
After Pops passed; yeah.
Well, Pops was living then and so that was in the early forties, and so we went on this tour, and as I said, I hadn't thought about Dewey, any connection and I was booked for a

black dance, an all colored dance, on a Thursday night, and I went on down--if you've ever been in that area, Seaside, Oregon, and we went on down to Seaside, Oregon Friday night and then we were back to Portland that Saturday for an all white dance.

So I guess maybe we were playing for about a half hour or more and I got a call-- I wouldn't like to be disturbed on the bandstand and I told them if anybody called that I'm just busy, unless it's very important, don't call me off the bandstand, and that's the order that I had given.

And so, Dewey Goosby began to call and they would always tell him he's busy, during intermission leave your number and he'll call you. And Dewey would say I'll call later. He wouldn't leave his name or anything, just say that he would call later.
So finally I got a call and they said it's long distance, Bernice Fields calling. Dewey knew my wife's name and everything, so I
got off the bandstand and Dewey said--I'll say it just like he said it--I knew I'd get your black ass off that bandstand if I told them your wife was calling.

So I said I was glad to hear from him but I still didn't know what he was going to say. So he says I know you're for nothing but the negro race, I want you to tell them they got to let us in there. We don't want to come in free, but we want to pay our admission and they don't want to admit us. So I said Dewey, you're putting me on the spot. He said what do you mean, putting you on the spot. I said I was here Thursday night and we had a negro dance, why weren't you here then? And I said I even stayed all night and didn't leave here until Friday, just in time to go to Seaside, Oregon, I would have been glad to visit with you, tight as we were and everything.
Well, this stuff that we can't go and I know you can tell them to let us in, we have our money and we got to break down this

junk and I said I'm for it, but you know what I wish you would do, why don't you get your bunch together and anybody that's playing, when one of these country and western bands are playing, come up and tell them that you want to come in and then lay down your money; but I said you want to break in when I'm coming, don't you know how they're going to treat that. Pops McElroy won't want no more negro bands in then.
Yeah, he just wouldn't hire any black bands.

That's it exactly. And so he finally acknowledged, he finally saw the point that I was talking about, so after he saw that, I said, I'll tell you what, we seem to be together now and I think Pops McElroy is okay, I said I'm going to talk to him and not only will I see that you get in, but you can get in, you and your party and won't have to pay a penny. Well, all right, but that won't mean anything unless we--I said that's all right, what it means, but I'm going
to see that you get in the dance, so you bring them on down.

So then I spoke to Pops McElroy and told him that my friend from Oklahoma was down and he wanted to bring a party in, I said I don't know how many they are. Pops McElroy said bring in whoever you want.
Pops was a fine man.
Yes, very fine.

So Dewey came on down, brought his party, I think four or five of them, but everybody was nice and happy and then I finally told Pops what he said and he said well, I'm with him, but you told him exactly right. He said what they need to do is come anything, when I got any band, they don't have to wait until I have a negro band, when I have anybody come on down and demand admission to the thing and he said then we will get this thing straight-ened out.
And so everything was happy and he went on out after the dance and we parted,
Now, what was his name?
Dewey Goosby, from Enid, Oklahoma originally and during World War II he was out working in the shipyard.
Where is Dewey now; is he still living?
I frankly don't know, but I know a few years back he was, because he came back to Oklahoma.
Now Ernie, you had a large number, as you said earlier, of outstanding musicians, who went on to become big names, especially saxophonists.
Yeah.
Teddy Edwards was in your band; Yusef Lateef who was known as Bill Evans.
Yeah, and Bill Evans not only, but Bill Evans was responsible really

for a very fine trumpet player, Julius Watkins; a trumpet and french horn. I always liked to be different, when a young man was wanting to join or I was auditioning anybody, when he had some doubles, that's when it attracted my attention, and so Bill Evans it was then, when he first started, like musicians will do, he kind of liked the group so he said if you ever need a trumpet man I have someone I would like for you to have and he recommended Julius Watkins and he went on to explain to me about him doubling on french horn. So as soon as I had a trumpet opening, I got Julius and Julius spent quite a while in the band and the last report I had of him he had joined a symphony in New York City on french horn.
You had Leroy Cooper, the great baritone man who went on to be with Ray Charles.
Yes, he went on to be Ray Charles' band director.
I worked in the band
with him, but he wasn't the leader when I was in the band. Edgar Willis was. But we had a great rapport.

Really, Leroy Cooper was one of my favorites among the sax that I did have, because he was just--why I lasted as long as I did, all along I would try to play for people. Now I liked when I had a musician if he was way out that was all right, but we're not going to do that all night, and I would try and look over the crowd; I would even have my book before I met the crowd to get all elements. So Leroy looked like he was a youngster but he could catch on to what I was meaning.
Play whatever piece it was.
Yeah, that's it. I remember we had a formal dance coming up and I knew they were going to want this dance, put your little foot; so I got to talking with some of the guys and they said oh,
Some of the guys said it was corny?

Yeah. Leroy said if that's what they want, let's get it. That's the way Leroy was and I don't remember exactly, but I think Leroy was in the band about three years when he was inducted in the service, World War II, out of my band.
I think Leroy Cooper is one of the least recognized lead saxophone players; I think he's the most underrated saxophonist that I've ever known.

I think so too. I'll tell you a youngster (inaudible) while Leroy was in the band, a man who was about perhaps forty five, we were in New York, and I was still struggling to get another record session but it just looked like I couldn't get it, it was always something. When I talked to somebody I didn't like the way they wanted
me to record and I'd pass it up and go on and it was pretty hard; I had to hustle around with personal appearances to keep the name up.

Well anyway, Rene Hall was in New York City doing pretty well and had nice connections and I played the Apollo Theatre and was working in that area and I told Rene if there was some kind of way that I could get a session; he said I don't know, the syndicate is funny, unless some of them got a piece of your band or this and that and so on, and so finally he said, I'll tell you what, if you can pay for a session yourself, I have a friend that owns a studio, I know we're all union and everything, but we may bootleg a deal over there to pay for me, pay and record. So anyway, I said if we're going to do that, find me a couple of good men to go along.
So anyway, we went into New York and we met him in Jersey, the Regal Company, and we did an original, a couple of us got together and the band jammed around and we did a

number, an instrumental number featuring Cooper on baritone sax, and it went so well and everything, they were just tickled, we released it and Chambers--did you ever know Chambers the trombone player?
Dewey Chambers?
Yeah.
Yes.
Well Chambers was on this session.

So anyway, I never did see that record anywhere in the states, but I got hold a few, and years later, when Cooper was with Ray Charles and he happened to come to Tulsa and he was laughing about an incident when he was in Europe. He said some musician came backstage and had a magazine and went to looking around and asking everybody's name and getting autographs like they do from the musicians, and so they spoke to Chambers before they did him and they said, you used to be with Ernie Fields and Chambers said no, I know Ernie Fields, but
I never was in his band, I just know him indirectly. Maybe I met him, I don't know. And so he said why did you ask me that? He said I have one of the records that you're on.
He recorded with you?

Yeah, and he said it's a big hit here. Then he looked over and he said, who is Leroy Cooper and Leroy said yeah, I was with Ernie Fields several years and then he thought, he said, you know what it is Chambers, that session, you did that session.
Now are we talking about Henderson Chambers or Dewey Chambers? There were two.
Were both of them trombone men?
I'm not sure; it loses me at this moment.
I forget the first name, but it was Chambers on trombone.
So they had the recording in Europe and released it?

Yeah, and it was a big seller. He had this magazine, what they were saying about it and they said they had to leave but they would try their best to get one of those, because I don't know how mine got away--I did have a few, (inaudible) I didn't have a publisher to protect it. Now to show you what it meant by bootleg things sometimes, I tried to talk to some of these youngsters when they say they're going to make a record; I'll say one thing about Teddy McRae, I met him in 1939--is it McRae or McVey?
McRae.

McRae, yeah; Teddy McRae. When we recorded, they did a number for Hammond and the first thing he said is Ernie, what publisher you going to put this with? Anyway, he opened my eyes on how to do that and we did that, and believe it or not, this is eighty one, and I believe last June I

got a check on one of the numbers, Jubilee Swing, that I did in 1939 from Europe, from London; it wasn't much but it goes to show you when anything is done right what it means. I think it was a dollar and eighty one cents or something.
Now, let's go on. You had Booker Ervin in the band?

Yeah. Now Booker Ervin is Dallas. You talk about this Dallas style, there's something about it. Somebody opened my eyes--when I had that incident in 1939 about Amos Woodruff--so I got to talking and needed a sax man. I was asked what kind of man and I said I definitely wanted somebody that can improvise and still have a good tone and some soul. I don't want somebody just blowing notes.
And so, we were in Dallas, Texas and Buster Bailey--I mean Buster Smith--who had been with Basie a long time, and Buster incidentally had done a lot of work for me and so

he says there's a youngster Ernie, who will fit, and I don't know what you're talking about, in Denison, Texas. So I got hold of Booker and he joined the band, and Booker just turned out to have that style that so many of them had coming from that area, a great big tone--if you remember Herschel Evans.
Yeah, swing.
And swing right on out and was very good on all of them, but I used him on baritone and tenor, and certainly tenor was his main instrument.
How long did Booker stay with you?
I imagine at least a couple of years.
Now, Don Byas worked in your band?
Yes, now Don Byas didn't work in the band too much after he was just sure enough things were going, but Don Byas and I broke bread together. You see, Don

Byas was from Muskogee, that's his home, and that's only sixty miles from Tulsa and then all of those youngsters around there want to say that they made a few dates with me, and terrific, I saw his talent from the beginning and he was great and I predicted that he would be one of the big ones and he sure did turn out to be.
Don and I worked briefly with Basie in 1943, we roomed together in fact. He was one of the great saxophonists. Did you know how he died?
No.
He died in Austria, I think it was, he was a mailman. He got to drinking very badly and I don't think they were hiring him much, but he was a postman.
It's just so bad how the whiskey messes up so many.
Don got onto that badly. Of course, he was an ex-patriot living in Europe for thirty years practically; he never came back
to the United States but once after many years in Europe.
Now, Candy Johnson, he used to mention you; I knew him well. He was a great tenor player who worked with Basie. How long did Candy work with you?

Not too long. Candy didn't work--I picked him up in Ohio, I forget what town it was, and I would say maybe a season or a tour, like we'd make these tours, and then a little later after that I heard he was with Basie; I don't know how long he stayed with Basie.
Not long. 1951 I think it was.
Since then Candy has visited me and he's married and doing fine. I think he's teaching.
I hope we have enough tape so we won't have to interrupt, one of the most interesting stories is the story of how "In The Mood" happened.
Well, before you go talking about that, I want to mention one more man before we got onto "In The Mood".

You spoke about him before, Teddy Edwards. Teddy Edwards--I had a habit--I don't have a lot, you know you can't take it with you, but I think I would have been more successful with money if I could just pass up a good musician, but when I saw a good one I couldn't pass it up. Do you know King Kolax?
Very well.
Well Kolax was in a band once but some people say that was a habit King Kolax had--he would have maybe twelve or fifteen people and didn't need them, but if they were good that was it.

So this thing about Teddy Edwards, I was looking for a guitar player and somebody had gone down south and inquired because as you say, (inaudible), and I was told about Jack Scott--Ernest Scott is his real name but he's known as Jack Scott--a guitar player, arranger,

and also he played piano, and so I talked with Jack and he was for it. I think it was in Jackson, Mississippi but they were originally out of Laurel, Mississippi and talked around, so you know how some of these guys are, I don't like to get into it, but like that buddy, you got to hire one with the other, but at the same time, I went to this little gig that they were playing, and I tell you the truth, I was just carried away with Teddy Edwards and so, they didn't have to influence me much about getting Teddy when Jack said now I'll go but Teddy wants to join you too.

I kind of played hard to get but I was glad to say yeah and I sent back later and got Jack and Teddy Edwards, and Teddy Edwards turned out just very sensational. I turned the reed section over to him and he worked with the guys. He was a nice musician; he could work with the brass men, but he meant a lot to my reed section.
I think I was the one that sug-
What was he playing with you?

He was playing alto, and then he picked up tenor a little there and I told him, I said Teddy, 'I believe you ought to stick with it. Did you know we lost Teddy a couple of years ago, he was very, very ill.
Yes, I know. I did a lot of work with him.
That's when he left the band, I can't blame him, you know, the travelling and he saw he could make it in one place.

Yeah, his name was Bill Evans. We mentioned him before and he brought Julius Watkins, and he was another guy-- I tell you what though, he was studying but he

He became a black Muslim.
Yeah, that was it. And so a few years after he had left the band he became Yusef.
He was here in Omaha in 1948.
He was?
He ran a band called Bob Nora, and he was the bandleader, more or less. He had a new Desoto limousine and I got to know him well.
I was a little surprised to learn that Bill Evans was Yusef Lateef.
Now, would you like to go on "In The Mood?"
Have we taken in all those sax men?
Yes. Can you think of anyone else?

I was trying to think. We mentioned Candy Johnson. While we're talking about fine sax men who have been through the band, I mentioned something about Artis Paul. Sometimes you wouldn't get the best of Artis, but I think he got onto whiskey-- he's gone on now like all the rest of us have to do someday--but he was just awful bad on the whiskey.
He was moody.
Yeah, a moody guy, but a fine, fine note man. I think I showed you

a picture of Stan Kenton with myself, and we were listening to a playback--well, that was when Stan was attracted. He said who is making those high notes. Well, Artis Paul was on that session there and Stan Kenton was so impressed-- some of them could make the high notes and may be out of tune.
He was pure.
You said it.
At different intervals, Artis was one of these come and go, he would be--another fine southwestern band which I know you know well, maybe as much or more than me, was Nat Towles.

I was with Nat Towles' band with Artis, a large percentage of 1944. Unfortunately he didn't get the recognition or the acclaim that he deserved. In another day Stan Kenton would have taken him with his band because he was as good a high note man as there was in the country, Artis Paul was.
Oh, yes.
Artis would switch from Nat and back to me, because he would always demand that salary.
He always wanted a little more money, and got it.
Yeah. And frankly, when he was sober he was worth it.
I'm going to show you some pictures of Artis, excellent pictures of Artis (inaudible).
I'm trying to think of another brass man that came through. Some of the things we're talking about now is passed that area but do you remember Chief--Russell Moore?
Yeah.
I think one of the finest trombone men in the business.
Certainly.
He was in my band nearly four years.
Are you still friendly with him?
Yeah, I spent three days visiting him in eighty.
In New York?

Yes, in New York. He's doing well, and I have a letter from Chief and his wife, he was in Europe, he was going over with a Dixieland group this past summer. So Chief is well and doing fine, I think he has cataracs or something, but he's just doing fine. He has a lot of his weight down now, and as of last year Chief was doing very well.

Well, the one characteristic thing about you Ernie is that all the guys that ever worked with you always venerated you, they loved you. I never heard a guy speak bad of you, and I mean this sincerely. I know hundreds of guys, and Ernie, they loved you, so you must have been fair, you must have been honest, which all bandleaders are not, not all

bandleaders are liked. I can name you some that are hated and guys don't even like to mention the fact that they worked with them, but every one that ever worked with you, Ernie--Eli Wilinsky, the Jewish kid who worked with you.

He was very fine, and I enjoyed time with him, and the funniest thing about it, I think I told you when he first began, I had a white musician in twenty eight, and some say that Benny Goodman was the first to have a mixed band, but I had a mixed band in twenty eight--
Well, he wasn't first, if you came chronologically in front of him in twenty eight.
And he travelled with me. I have a picture--I had some when Eli was in the band but it may have gotten away, but I have one of Iller when he was in the band. He took Spurgeon West's place.
Iller?
Harold Iller. Yeah,
when I was trying to get you. He took the chair that I wanted you to. We had several incidents, but everything worked out fine with Harold.
I don't think we should touch on the "In The Mood" thing until we turn over the tape, because that's a long, interesting one, about how "In The Mood" came about.

I guess why they said that, I guess through some vision I always knew that it was the band that was the show and if you look at some of the press material, I never was any sensational soloist and never did try, but I didn't try to be a one-man band, and they would always say, when one had the ability, he was introduced and he was featured and even if he wasnt a star, I would let you know he was in my band, and I tried to always-- my arrangements, I would talk to them. One reason that I got along with Rene Hall, he arranged after he left and we were pretty tight, I would tell him how I would like for this to

be fixed when we were talking, and If I had a man in the band and if he was good enough to be in my band and he's getting paid (inaudible) and that's the way that I did and I would always let him know that if he was there, he was important.

That was one thing that I learned when I was first starting from T. Holder. If you're in there, you're not all that much better than the person you're sitting beside of and I guess when the men knew that that was the way I was, I guess they stood by me.

I heard you had a very colorful fellow, you did tell the most interesting story about Leon Wright taking the picture. Leon Wright was a fine showman and Bill Evans, they were my two tenor men, Bill Evans and Leon Wright and he would put on such a show, you'd have a battle of the saxes sometimes and poor Leon, compared with what Bill Evans played, was plain nothing, but he would steal the show from him everytime, and we would say Mr. Public
and Leon would do something (inaudible). As I said, I went for the jazz but I was going to put on something that I think would help bring the people in.
You would have a battle of the tenors between Leon and Bill Evans, Yusef Lateef and Leon would steal the show and he was nothing compared to him.

But Bill--Yusef, was very clever too and when he learned it, (inaudible). Yusef was a great, big guy and he would be blowing and blowing and Leon would spread his legs out wide and Leon would get off when he started blowing and just go through his legs and when he would do that the house would go loud. He was quite a showman.

Then we brought up another act, a young man, while we're talking about sax too, we've been talking about those great soloists, but a very fine first alto man was Harold Minerve who now is with the Duke Ellington Band and has been for some years even before Duke

passed. He had a little act that he and Leon used to do together. Leon would put on a dress and they used to do this--remember when Smoke That Cigarette--some country and western band had that--but anyway we had a novelty deal on that and Leon and Harold--Geesil--would put on this act, Leon would have on a dress and so one time I asked him, how did you think of that. He said I used to do this for years and he said-- what's this big comedian--
Flip Phillips--Flip Wilson.
Flip Wilson.
He said he got that idea from me. He said before I even was in your band I did. He was originally from the east somewhere and he said Flip got that from him.

Look at the picture of him, long before Flip Wilson became famous, it is unbelievable, but it's just like he's doing-- Leon looks like he's doing that Geraldine routine and that came long before Flip Wilson
became famous, so it is possible that he's telling the truth.

And another thing, he would watch everything, and in the south--he would say a lot of things, but this wasn't anything malicious, but he had--I just wish I had the picture because it's just so comical to think how this race issue was so simple. I believe it was Tougaloo, Mississippi that we were playing, and Sammy Edwards, the drummer, very nice drummer, he didn't go on to be sensational but he was among one of the best drummers I had and we had--
