I believe it was Tougaloo, Mississippi that we played one night and Sammy Edwards, our drummer, had a terrible toothache, you could just see the misery he was in, so when I got off--we were playing a black dance--I said about a dentist. So they said we don't have a colored dentist here and two or three of them talked and talked and finally they decided well perhaps doctor so and so, a white dentist, he's pretty nice, maybe we can get him to pull his tooth tomorrow, see what he can do for him.

So early that next morning about opening time, I picked up Sammy and Leon Wright went along with me, and I don't know, Leon looked like he was saying something, he had his camera and the people went in there and talked to the dentist and told him this young man was in misery, would he look at him and see. So finally he said, well, I can't let him suffer

like that, if he doesn't mind it, I'll just move my regular chair out on the porch and I'll pull his tooth for him and do whatever I can for him, but I can't let him sit in my chair in my office and pull his tooth because suppose some other white person comes in while he's sitting in the chair; it would ruin me.

So we thought the main thing was to get Sammy out and do what he could and he gave him some kind of prescription to take after he pulled it. So he was very nice and went on and pulled it and he had a regular house chair on the porch and a towel around Sammy and Leon took the picture.
Did he ask the dentist?
Yeah, he asked the dentist and he said yeah, that's all right.

I said that was one thing that I wanted to keep, I said get some of them made up and he said yes and as things went on we separated but Leon was just a very nice fellow, always full of fun and before things woke up,

where you could be served anywhere, Leon wore an earring in his ear and we would go around and if we thought there was anything, we would go in a place of business and if we wanted service for something, maybe they would turn me down, especially this eating in there, and they would tell Leon they can't serve him, Leon would shake his head and say me no savvy, he didn't know what they were talking about and they'd go ahead and serve him.

They guys used to kid him and say someday some of those people are going to pull that earring out of your ear when you say you no savvy; but I've seen him get by with that several times. They would talk and tell him no and he would just shake his head and they'd go on and do whatever he asked for.

About that servicing, I was in the south once before, on the edge of some little town and they had this little general store like they have so many places now, you'd get what you want and come to the cash register, and we saw

that that was the kind of place it was and we went on in and got whatever we wanted and went to the cash register and paid for it, and some youngsters, negro boys, were in there and they did the same thing, they went to the cash register and they paid the man. So when they were paying, we were still in there and so the white fellow said to them, now, you ought to know better than that; those folks don't know any better and said now, that's all right this time, but when you come back here again now, do like you always do, ask for what you want and we'll go get it for you. And so the youngsters said thank you and they went on out and so while we were out, we were fooling around before we left and were getting on the bus, one of them looked up and saw the name on the front, we had it in the front of the bus, like they have towns, and I had Ernie Fields. One of the boys said, I never heard of that town. Another one of the boys said I haven't either, but I know one thing, it must be up north.

You see, the fellow in the store said they were from somewhere else and they don't know what you're supposed to do, so the kids figured you could do different up north, so they said wherever that is, that's up north.
Ernie, in your bus, did you have the usual fun going on, the games and jokes, the card games, and I presume they shot a little dice?
Oh, sure.
Did you take part in the fun?

Well it's a funny thing, believe it or not, I don't know if I mentioned, I guess you'll say what else about T. Holder; well I learned a lot of good things and I don't know if that was bad, T. Holder turned me against gambling because that's the way he lost his band. You see, I knew him personally and he lost the 12 Clouds of Joy gambling and in the band so many guys would gamble and drink, they would get broke and begging
and so I would figure that maybe if I was lucky and win, they'll figure I should owe them some money then and so I always stayed out of it.
Of course if they lost their money, they'd blame you because they didn't have money. It would be your responsibility.
But I mean the fun and the games.

Oh, yeah, we had that and I would be in there and it would knock them out how some of them would arrange it, they would do so much of that and it was all in fun and you know, after all, you've got to do something. Those long rides and everything; you'd go nuts if you didn't do something.
Was Clarice the dancer with you?
Yes.
What was her last name?
Clarice Ford.
A cute little thing.
Eli told me some stories about

how some of the guys got into a fight over her This Deek Wilson--it wasn't really a fighting over some other member of the group, but this Deek was going with Clarice and if some outsider--you know you've got to be good and courteous and everything and especially when she made up and everything, she was in this dance act with a one legged dancer, you know, and if some young man or something smiled at Clarice too much, Deek would go and knock him in the head, and it just got to be ridiculous.
It was so much trouble--he was a nice trumpet player too, but I had to talk to Deek, but the young man, if the moon changed he would change.
Thomas?
Thomas Wilson.
He worked with my band for about a year; I had to let him go for the same reason, he was very violent. He cut one of the busdrivers, a big cut out of his hand
and he had a girl travelling with him and he beat up on her in the bus. So he was jealous about Clarice?
Yeah (inaudible) would say would you like to go to dinner tonight,
And she had to mix with the crowd.
No, not with Deek. And as I said, when that moon changed you'd just have to look out.
Yeah, they said he changed with the moon. I think there was some kind of werewolf in there or something.
He's still in Tulsa now.
I know.
He's working and doing very well.
One reason I had to let him go, he could have easily killed somebody or hurt somebody or I to him; I had to shoot a pistol over his head one time and tell him the next one
was him.
I heard about that.
But now I don't believe I have a better friend, he's working (inaudible), he says, if anything happens to me, call Ernie.
Is that right?

Yeah, that's right. And sometime ago, I don't know what Deek does for amusement around, but Deek just works, works, works and he had a sick spell and they had to rush him to the hospital and they had on there, call Ernie Fields and when I went out, he said I told them to get ahold of you and talk to the doctor and there wasn't anything but rest for him.

Well, I fired him, I fired him at Rapid City, South Dakota. He left me and worked for a few weeks or a month for a tailor shop and then he went directly to you, and I said, oh lord, poor Ernie. But that's all the past and it's a miracle that Deek wasn't
in a situation where someone killed him or he killed someone.
Yeah, but you know, that's one thing that I can say, out of those thirty or thirty five years, as many different characters that I worked with, I got along with them pretty nice.
You never had any violent situations with any of your men?
No, no, never.
They did respect you and as I said, venerated you so, but even so, there's always some violent people.
Yes, always.

In fact, a young man that's here now in Omaha, Basie Gillens, he was saying that long ago he would hear some of the guys talking and said anybody that come from that area, and especially when they would get to talking about money--none of us were making anything that amounted to anything, we got ten or twelve dollars guaranteed, and we were happy if that

was guaranteed for a night, but some of them would even take that and Basie said before he knew me and everything, some of the guys would say, well, let's try Ernie, and somebody who had been in the band would say, well, that's one thing about him, he'll be fair with you and make you feel you.

Incidentally, I was told about Basie when I started booking and when I got a date with him I found out that he was certainly a fine man to do business with, because the kind of band that he had, he played for the people.

Well, I worked with Basie Gibbens' band when I first came back from Count Basie's band, 1948; I worked the whole summer with him, and I still enjoyed a great friendship with Basie Gibbens; Elmer is his real name.
I renewed my friendship at the convention.
I was visiting one of the board members of the union--for several years I've

been going to the national convention--and I got acquainted with Basie and he brought back remembrances and this and that and so on and we've been very close the last few years and since we're speaking about the union, he and discussed how it is, and frankly speaking, I think it's getting weak. You know, it's all right, but I wonder about it. It's away from the playing, but I will say this, I feel great that I got over one by-law this past year in our local.

I contended and fought that we need something in our by-laws other than what you can't do. Everything you open the union has don't do this and don't do this and so how I came to this, I would be in contact with musicians, with youngsters and I would say why don't you join the union, by being a booking agent; well, we finally got it over you can book whatever you wish, but I would kind of encourage them to be in the union and they would just say well, what's the need, they don't do anything

for you.
So finally a new club, two or three years ago, opened up in Tulsa, Zigfields, and a boy got a gig in there, a nice paying gig, right locally, which you know yourself, about twenty five hundred a week right there on location, and they had some kind of trouble with the crowd and he fired him without notice, and the boy filed charges, and he got on the burner, he was just very intense about the way it was done and everything and they still refused to pay him, they weren't going to pay him. The put the club on default and the club turned around then and filed charges against him and this thing had to be fought out in court and put a strain on ninety four.
The union?
The union there, on ninety four and Tony Twist, the leader.
So then, to protect their own skin, the union had to fight. Well, we won it, but it cost money and so I brought it up after that that
in our by-laws that anytime a contract was deposited and everything was as it should be and they they couldn't get it, (inaudible) that they go to civil court and at the local's expense.

The secretary kind of didn't know and this and that, but finally they put it on three reasons, and it went overwhelmingly that in other words--and I explained to them--I said we had this past example that--we didn't know whether Tony Twist was going to win that--and of course the secretary said, before it was passed, what are you trying to do, break the union? He said, do you know how much that lawsuit cost? I said that's a point to have something to show in there that we do for the musicians.
Who was Tony Twist?
That was the orchestra leader that filed the lawsuit against Zigfields.
Tony Twist?

Yes, he filed charges against Zigfields and of course, he was right and they put Zigfields on default, but then Zigfields turned around and put the union on restrainer, that they couldn't do this. So we went to court.
Did he get his money, did Tony Twist get his money?
Yeah. The filed for the two weeks work, you know, (inaudible). But the whole point was that when I got over there and that vote came up, it went over overwhelmingly.

I could remember about the union, as I said, how come unions--you see, unions used to be strong you might say in the twenties and thirties, and especially for the blacks, because so many didn't belong, and when I began to play around and attract a little attention, well, I'd send somebody for work and they'd ask, are you union, and it was good to have. So I inquired around and we
couldn't join the local, but I could join Dallas or Kansas City, that was the nearest one to me, the black local--
You didn't have a black local in Tulsa then?
No.

I am the charter member of the Tulsa black local when we had to have it, and so what I did I joined 168 in Dallas, Texas; Bernie Johnson was secretary then and went on for several years, and then when it came this ten percent tax, that was a big headache, if you were out of that jurisdiction, you had to pay that ten percent tax.
So I would come home and go play and there was Danny Fox--he was the secretary of ninety four.
Danny Fox?
Yeah, Fox; everybody called him Danny Fox. And oh, he was a fox too.
So I'd say I live here; well, you don't belong here, 168.

So I went into Dallas and got to talking to Bernie one time and he said, Ernie, I think I have about fourteen pieces in the band, you have enough people; I think all you need is twelve people and he said the nice thing about it, with your band is, if there is somebody else around there that would like to be union, some of the teachers or this or that or something, and so I came back and started talking around and Spurgeon West was president of our first local; A.G. Rogers who was a teacher there was a musician and I believe Charles Roberts, another guy, and we got in and we sent in and 808.
That was your black local number?
Yeah; 808.
So we went on for years and years until the law came down that you had to merge.
So you merged?
Oh yeah, we merged.
What do you call it?
It's 94. We don't call it 808 and 94, we're all in 94.
Wonderful. Now what are you?
I'm on the board of 94.
You go to conventions?
Yes, I go to conventions. I'll tell you about the convention-- since we are talking about union--I think he's dead now--who was your president?
Charlie Williamson.
He passed a couple of years ago?
That's right.
Well, Williamson--he was on his P's and Q's.
He sure was.
Well I had been going to the national but it wasn't any law that I had to go, you know, that they had to see me or any-
thing like that, although I had been on the board several years.

One year the vice president of our local, they had president, vice president and treasurer, by the by-laws, three would go. And so, this vice had open heart surgery and couldn't go, so they sent me in his place, and I'll never forget, we were in Hawaii and I was tickled to death to get that ride to Hawaii and so we went there and Williamson, on the last day of the convention and he came out, he said Fields, I don't remember the number of the resolution--he said, we got to see that this is passed today, and I said what's that, William? So he showed it to me and it was that any man that blacks have offered to this profession and this and that and since we don't have black locals, it must be a law that local that is merged by the law, well they must send a black whether he is an officer or not; they must send a black.
Well, I'll be.

So that was in there, and so I said I'm glad you join that attention and he said the only thing about it, it never had come up and he said today is the last day, this was early in the morning, he said we've got to see--we were just waiting around before the meeting was over--during the meeting those five days, I'd been figuring a few that were pretty good speakers, white and black, I was noticing, so I got around to a few of them and told them, look here, we got to see that this comes up, and the funny thing, everyone that I spoke to, they said, do you know that they've been evading this for about three years and I say yeah, that's what I understand.

All this was before the meeting was open, so when it opened we got to our seats and my secretary came in and the president and of course I was in there, I was delegate, as vice president. So I turned to my secretary and said this has to come and he looked up and said, oh yeah, but Fields if we bring this up,

Ernie, and pass a law like this, what is the Indian going to say, the Mexican going to say or the Jew going to say; they're going to say you've got to see that they count as well as that. I didn't say anything, but we always got along fine, but I said then, what does my secretary think, I'm ignorant? What is the connection with that? The deal definitely said that we had to merge and so I didn't say anything--
In the first place, there were no Indians or Mexican locals; there had been black locals and a white local.
That's it.

So anyway, when that went to come up I got up, I was near mike seven, when I got up the secretary and president almost turned white, they wondered what I was going to say. So many were jumping for it, white and black, and so I got to standing there so long, one guy next to me was going around and I started going back and they said no, don't leave and another
guy gave me a seat right next to that number seven where I was out.

So directly, the chairman was watching and finally he said, number seven and when I got up I said to myself, I'm going to set my president at ease. The first thing I said was Local 94 and I said you take 94, I don't believe there's any local that white and black get along any better or as well as we do, it's just fine. I said but do you know why I'm here? The man said no. I said by accident. I said I never would have been a delegate if the vice president hadn't been ill; he couldn't make it and I'm here as his substitute, but I said yes, we want a vote and get this passed so that me or somebody from ninety four can always be here, and boy, the people just yelled.

So finally it was going so much, they finally said do we have to have a rollcall on that and so they finally said no--I'm trying to think who was president then--the national president, and it looked like he was trying to

evade it and so some lady that was on that committee said, Mr. President, I was on the committee that brought this up three years ago--a white lady from somewhere out in Louisiana that said that, and she said when I brought it up, everybody thought just fine, but every year since then we're too busy to get to it, and said we're not going to pass it this year. Whatever kind of time, we're going to pass this before we go into anything.
And so they finally said we don't have rollcall, that would take too much and they put a motion all in favor and the whole house just stood up and hollered yes.
There was one little guy from Florida--it was unanimous--and he said well, I never stood up and everybody just fell out. But it went over.
So you've got to have a black representative--
Yeah, it doesn't matter whether he's an officer or not, because
they said they had to do something, it was just dwindling down (inaudible).

You mentioned earlier that the union has been weakened lately; it certainly has, at this level, your smaller towns; not in Los Angeles and New York, big cities where you have studio work they're strong, but in these little towns like here the unions are terrible.
Definitely so, and really, believe it or not Preston, it's a little weak, I think, even in the larger towns. We have a black secretary out there, Marvin Young,--
We have a vice president.

I'll tell you about a coincidence--you know, he's a fine musician too--and when he was in Chicago, before he went, he's hard working and very clever, you know, he's an attorney, but when he was in Chicago, some kind of way--what's that club, Club DeLisa?
Yeah.

I think I was playing there once and got acquainted with him, he had an act or something and I did a number and I kind of liked it, and at that time I spoke to him and told him I liked it. He said do you want it? I said I would like to have this arrangement and he said I'll bring you one. I said what do I owe you; just tell them where you got him, let me do some arranging and he did become a very nice arranger.
Well you know, Marv was the music director for a time for the Lucy Show.
Yeah. And another well known musician, a brass man, a trombone man and writer, J.J. Johnson. He finally got straightened.
Yeah; we worked with Basie together, 1945. J.J. is all straight, I think he wrote the music for Shaft.
That's what I was

telling you about, his writing. The way I went into New York City and was working that area for a while and had to augment the band, I had been recommended about J.J.--I tell you who first told me about him, I heard of him but had never met him, was Clarence Little. He came from Indianapolis, the Ferguson Brothers, a booking outfit. I think he used to book Clarence and he was almost a part of them and so J.J.--he told me J.J.'s a good writer or something, and he said if you can find him and so when I finally did find out about him in New York, they told me he's a fine musician, instrumentalist and arranger if you get him straight.
You're referring to (inaudible)
Yeah.
And so he joined the group and was with me--not for long, but several weeks, and we got very tight and he gave me some arrangements. You see, if you weren't in that big
money, those arrangements cost you. So J.J. said I'm just glad you're doing this work and said see if you can tell somebody about my writing.

Getting back to Charlie Williamson, you know he played with King Oliver, trumpet and we have an American Legion Post named after him now. Charlie Williamson American Legion Post--I forget the number--and he's been dead around three years. Of course I went to his funeral; he was a great musician.
Yes.
And he became a key union man. He was an authority on union by-laws.

But I'll never forget, we were going in early that morning and he told me--of course I had got acquainted with him before, he said we have to get this. One other thing--but ask what you want while I'm thing about what I wanted to say.
Look at this pictures and since we're going to get to that In The Mood
thing, there's Plas Johnson, there's your son, Ernie, Jr., there's Earl Palmer and Rene Hall and yourself. Of course those three guys-- Earl Palmer was the number one drummer for years.
Oh, yeah.
Plas Johnson and Rene has his own musical service and now your son is out there doing well.
The story, In The Mood, you tell it just like you told me, you know rumors change things, but I learned the story almost exactly like you told it. That story I'm very interested to get to.
Yeah.

Well, all along Rene Hall and I had been very close friends and he did arrangements for me even after he was out of the band. One time he was with Earl Hines band and Earl had--you see the big bands had slow times as well as the little ones, and I had a nice run down in Dallas, and I was on a location and so I called up Rene and told him what's Earl doing?
He said we've been off for a while. I said let me send for you to come down to Dallas. He came down and worked a while with me arranging and everything and went on back--
What year was this?
That was in the forties still.

But indirectly all along, we would get along and I'd call up Rene and we'd write once in a while and I'd say how you doing, I said, Rene, I'm just trying my best to hold on until Junior gets out of school because nothing is going to do him but being a musician and I want to be of a little help to him. I said since he chooses to take it I want to do all I can for him.

You see originally, since we're talking about this, I didn't want my son to be a musician, although I started him taking piano lessons at five years old and right on, then when he picked up a saxophone I went and bought
him a clarinet and said I want you to learn this clarinet first, and then got him a special teacher for that.
So when he went away, after he finished high school, he had a scholarship for Texas College from Tyler, Texas. That's where Leroy Cooper and a lot of those boys came from.

So he went down there and it was right on the verge of World War II and I said,-- he got to bugging me, dad, I want to change school. I wanted him to be a doctor or a lawyer, I said there's nothing wrong with music, if I thought there was anything wrong I wouldn't be one myself, but I said you got to be good and you got to be lucky. I said I'm not worried about you being good, but I'm wondering will you be lucky.

Anyway, he said okay and he said what about going to Howard and I said what? He said when I come home from midterm, let me go to Howard and I'll write and see if I can get in there and he said I'll go in for pre-med
and he said at the same time they have ROTC department, and he said maybe I can finish school before two years.
So at midterm he went on to Howard
Howard in Washington?
Yes.
Howard University?
Washington, D.C.

He entered there and when he came back he started on me again I want to get in the music department. But I said lose a year over there and he laughed, and he said I met the head of the music department and he grilled me a little. He told me when I come back that could be my major and he'll start me as second year. He said I already know enough for that first year.

So I said well it's your life, whatever you want you do. So then he was in as a music major and then I began to check again on him and he was good in everything but they were about to put him out of school for missing ROTC.

So anyway, I said Rene, you know Junior is majoring in music and so he'll be trying to have a band and I'd like to stay in it until he gets out and I said it's just so tough on the road though, if you don't have a record or this or that it's just so hard. He said I'm connected up pretty good, I can't guarantee you no hit but I can get you a session, because I'm pretty well known out here.
So I said okay, we'll look forward to it if we can. So I was in Seattle, Washington and I said, Rene, I think I'm going to come through--
This is much later?
Yes, some months later, around fifty eight.
I said I was coming on down through there, and I was working out of Seattle and I had some pretty nice men in there, Oscar Estelle--did you know him?
Certainly.
Lionel got him out
of my band. And Elon Watkins.
Oscar played?
Alto.
And Elon Watkins played?
Tenor.

They were in the band at that time and so I said I was going on down through L.A. and Rene said to me, I tell you what, it would be good if you had some original material, let's see what you have and send it and if you don't, he said I can get a lot and so on and so forth, and so anyway, I got to talking while we happened to be working out of the area and I got acquainted with a fellow who, as a hobby, was studying, was taping and recording and all and he had a good system, stereo and all and had all the mikes for each instrument and so I got him to make several numbers for him.
In Seattle?
In Seattle.
And I sent them off to Rene and I said listen to them before I get down there and
I think we should add here that Rene had a big office, a music office in recording, music writing, copying service, in Hollywood, so he's established now.
Yes.
You had sent him this material?

Yeah, and I called him up, I said Rene, what did you think about the material? He said what's wrong with your band, I don't know you to have a band like that, how that sounds. I just can't get any kind of sound out of it, I don't know what's going on there and I went on and said I can't understand and I went on to name some of the guys. Rene said I had some pretty nice guys in the band and
he said we'll check, you'll see what I'm talking about when you get here.

So when we went to L.A., he took me to the studio to see what he was talking about and when they played it he pointed and (inaudible). So I said what kind of machine are you playing it on and he went on to say mono and I said this is in stereo (inaudible).
Stereo was new.
Yeah.
Then he made some studio where he could do it and we went on then and played and Rene just flipped over it.

I had a couple of vocal numbers on there, I think I had something on Ann Walls there and he said now, you do what you want, Ernie, but you know you've had one of the greatest vocalists--he was talking about Melvin--but he said I think what you need to do is get some of this instrumental, he said you got some nice instrumental numbers here, but get some of this instrumental (inaudible). He said you'd be
smarter maybe if you recorded it alone, but as far as you let it be just Ernie Fields.
Yes, because a vocalist is independent of the bandleader.
So the way the time was, he said he'll take time, we'll do it as I see how you have something. I said yes, as long as I have a band I'm going to have something.

So anyway, he said, I'll tell you what, after the first of the year, I know to be exact--that was in fifty eight--he said you come on out, we'll get together and do that. So we went on and I think the next thing we were playing was Williams Air Force Base, we were coming on back east, one night, whatever it was, and a little incident happened there.
During our career we had a lot of them, this race deal--

Yes, Williams Air Force Base in Williams, Arizona. We played the officer's club and we went in and the fans, they were practically hugging and kissing you but when we got through with the dance, everything was closed on the base, so we came on through in the little town and found us an all-night cafe, so we walked in and sat down. Nobody came to us and said we're not going to serve you or what will you have, or anything. We just sat there. Finally, this white fellow turned around and said, was anybody here in the Army, in the service? And Wallace Wilson was one-- I think I had two that had been in, I don't know if you knew Wallace Wilson, he was from New York City--I don't know originally but that was where
What did he play?
Trumpet. He was once with Sonny Finnegan, this jazz band, a fine musician.
The white guy said that?
Yeah.

Yeah, that's what I had this little deal that I said, when I was reading that to you, I consider him responsible for that hit. I have it on something about that.

Yeah.

I kind of had a little malice because that twenty five would have meant so much to me and I thought that he should--

He didn't.

I said I can't sing and he said, now don't say that. I said why do you

say that? He said, I used to say that. He said I had a big band once and he said, I said I couldn't sing. The band broke up, I went and got a job with a trio and just playing an instrument but when the guy came up and said we had to sing I went jiving around because the man said if I played there I had to sing some. So that's the way this trio started and I always said I couldn't sing. And believe it or not, they are fixing now, to put me out as a singer.

And so just like we were talking, I got to talking to Parker and told him that they were going to put Nat out as a singer and he said, I'll be damned, he got away with that trio stuff and he ain't strong enough to be no singer, and then he named somebody else in the trio (inaudible).
About another six months later, they had a recording out about Nat King and there was no turning back.
Another time, Nat King was in Denver, I did a one-nighter, Bill Jones booked

So Nat said you don't think I play any jazz? So he said, I don't think you do. He said now I like your playing, I was just wondering why you don't play some jazz. He said, well now, to make you know that I'm playing jazz, like everyone else, maybe I didn't have on one of them little beaver pelts and was looking just straight ahead, not looking around at nobody at what's going on or nothing, but I stared and played away and then maybe you would think I'm playing jazz.
So the guy got a laugh and said, well, maybe so. He said I'll tell you what, those different things, even just a little tinted

He said before I married, he said I went to visit my wife--they weren't married-- he was engaged and everything and he told him that he told his daughter that I've seen you before and I just thought you were going wrong, I didn't know if you were hiding and don't want nobody to see your eyes, but you're going around with those dark glasses. So he said he just smiled and said, well, I'm not going to change my glasses, I work in front of lights and these are not really dark glasses, they're just tinted a little so I can see and don't have the glare of the lights.

Great jazz player.

And then another--as I said perhaps so many in between, almost too numerous to name, but one I will not pass up, was Harry Burns. It was kind of odd and strange the way it came about. Did I ever say anything to you about the incident about the guy who said you

No, you didn't tell me that, but first, you did tell me Herb Burns' name was something else.

Yeah.

So Rene then said to me, I guess you see what I'm talking about.
That's why he didn't
want to come south with you.
Yeah.

Yeah, Rene was still with me then. He was with the band eight years. So anyway, I went on back and I got a call from Burns again maybe a month or two later and he was sending me in a different direction this time. Yeah, he was a salesman.

I finally got a hold of him and he said, yeah, I remember that, forget about it. If he wants another date, tell him I'll contact him and he can have another date and if he advertises or something, I'll pay for that from my commission.
That was Ft. Lauderdale?
Yeah, Ft. Lauderdale.
Did you play the Ft.
I didn't right then because it was too close and Burns had gone on and he had me on another date that I had to go on.
That same night?
Yeah, yeah. I went on but I did finally come back and played Ft. Lauderdale and everything was fine.

At that time everything--it wasn't like it is now, so many bands don't even have a piano, they have the little portable and so we played one place--before I quit the business I used to (inaudible), but at that time I didn't think about it, I would usually inquire if the piano was in tune where I was playing, but here I was playing somewhere and the fellow, when we went in, told me they didn't have any piano, don't need one (inaudible).
We played a place once that had been a (inaudible), and the man told us, I

intend to start to having dances here, but we haven't had time to map the floor, and Burns-- I don't know what kind of line he told people, but he was persuading those people that don't worry about a thing, that we carried something along to have a floor.
So we went and set up and everything and looked down there and they said, that fellow that booked said you all have something that wasn't very big, but he said we would have a small space to dance.
So we went on with the dance and folks were dancing (inaudible).

We made this round on and on and I will say that I have a write up there that Burns is responsible for and we'll send that in to Ron too, The University of Miami. You see, by Burns booking the Wings over (inaudible), he just knew when they'd be in the south or when they'd be in the north and so he had got together with some youngsters at the University of Miami and they, I think, had said to him, well
A big prom?
Yeah.

So Burns said you can't miss this opportunity to get a terrific man like this, to play that homecoming, and he decided some kind of way that he would--Burns even told him where we would be--at that time I don't think he knew where we would be, I think he told him some kind of lie to where we'd be and it would be so far they'd have to fly us in, they'd have to pay more money to fly us in, and he got that extra money and we got that homecoming dance; there's a picture of me and student director and I have also a write up--Dr. Thurston Adams.
Yeah, you're shaking hands with him.
Then one of these
youngsters presented me with the check that night for flying the band in.
First black band to play--
Yeah, yeah, it's a write up in the paper there.

So Burns was just doing fine and was tickled and all until Burns went to taking money from those army bases and air force bases, and one thing about it, he never would (inaudible), I wouldn't know anything about the contract, and so a lot of it was return dates the second round, so they had had my name in all those places and they would call my wife, call my home, and say where's Ernie Fields, he's supposed to be here tonight. She said no, he's so and so, he's somewhere else. Well, we have a contract that he's supposed to be here and so, (inaudible).
You were in the clear?
Yeah, I was in the clear.

He just went on and did so many of those, and they turned the FBI on him, and when he found out that, a long time after that, I don't know what in the world happened, but I really wanted to find Burns, because he did a lot. It wasn't as big as some of the other agencies, like William Morris or Jim Artis, but it was so regular.
We worked so regular that sometimes we didn't have time to get laundry done.

We were in Frisco at the time and (inaudible)--we'd been working so steady, a very fine vocalist in the band and he told us that when we get back this time to headquarters--his headquarters was Kansas City--he said I'm going home and stay a while, we've been going at it and I've got to spend a little time at home.
He was married?
Yeah.
I told him okay then, and they were always very nice, he said I don't want to
put you on the spot, you start looking for somebody and so we were in Frisco and naturally the guys would make the joints a little more than I would and they ran across a young man, Al Harris--
I don't remember him.
He was with me a good while.

Al was pretty nice and when he left the band he got on the Playboy circuit as a singer; he was nice, he was all right. They found Al and Al said I'll have to give notice where I'm working, and he met me in Vernal, Utah. First we were saying Salt Lake City and he couldn't, but Burns had us in a number of towns in Utah, and he could find them, I don't know how he would do it, and so we were there and Al got there before we did and so he went in--he was just so nervous when we got in town, they jumped him, are you with Ernie Fields' band and he said yeah, and they said, where's Harry Burns? He said he didn't know anything

about no Harry Burns and they had a picture and they showed him and he said, I don't know anybody but Ernie Fields, and to tell you the truth, I have never played an engagement with him, I'm supposed to start off tonight with him. He heard me in Frisco--he went on to tell him-- and he said I'm joining him here tonight. He said I don't know anything about Harry Burns.

And so it looked like they seemed to think that maybe he was jiving because they went on to ask him, will Harry Burns be here tonight? He said I don't know, and he said I don't know anything. But the guy disappeared, but they found out later that he was somewhere but it where he could see whoever came to this hall.
The FBI?
Yeah, the FBI.
We came on and set up and Al was talking about it, and he was pretty nervous. He was kind of scared (inaudible), and I said no and he told me about this FBI and I said

well, maybe he's gone now. He said well I don't know. This guy, he thought that even after we were there that maybe Burns would show up, so then finally he came up and wanted to know about Harry Burns. I said I don't know. He said is he the one that booked you? I said yeah; so, where is he? I said right now I don't know. I said I would give you his home address.
Did you ever come across Harry Burns again?
No; and I looked for him, but I think he was so hot or something that he just gave it up.
So I told him, and this man told me then that they have tried that, but he's not in New Orleans now. So I really don't know.
Now, how many times did you play the Apollo? Quite a number of times?
Oh, yes, quite a number of times. I would say that I doubt if I missed a single year between thirty nine and

fifty. I then came back again a little after fifty, but between thirty nine and fifty, it was rather regular, and one thing about it, that's one reason that so many names that I got acquainted with--because sometime I learned if I had a good nucleus I could be playing but didn't have to (inaudible). That's when Gene Ammons worked that circuit with me.
He did?
Yeah.

I got acquainted with those guys and I told them how many weeks I wanted them and we (inaudible). That's where I first got a hold of Wallace Wilks, the trumpet player, and I believe the first time Bill Evans was working with the band.
Yusef Lateef.

I was thinking just for that time and Bill said no, man; you see, that was good dough then but I told him, if you want to be in the band I can't guarantee you that kind of money and it turned out they
The theatres were better than the dances.
Oh, sure.
And they were very, very good contacts.
Another thing that was good was this like the Red Caps--do you remember when they were hot?
Damita Jo.
And the Mills Brothers. I played with the Mills Brothers.

I'll tell you a coincidence with the Mills Brothers; I worked with them several times so when I was on the west coast there I turned short a lot--I mean to be frank, I didn't have as big a class music like I had a lot of times, but I was satisfying Mr. Public.
I had worked with the Mills Brothers several times back east and in Chicago and there was this number that I think Cab Calloway did--Sabre Dance--well, I had a Parker

Berry arrangement--oh, it was terrific and we had figured out a deal that just before they pull the curtain, we had the sabres in front of the stands and the lights and we did that show one time with the Mills Brothers. We took as many bows as the Mills Brothers.

So I was going up the west coast once, I think it was Coquille, Oregon, and sometimes these towns will try to bring in big things and so they had contacted the Mills Brothers for a dance, and so the Mills Brothers told them, well apparently the man gave two prices; if it's just the Mills Brothers or if we had to bring a back up band it's got to be so and so. So the guy told them, this gig that I want you for, we're making that a big affair, we have Ernie Fields in there. And so they told him, enough said.
They came into this town and they were in town, they notified us time for rehearsal, work out all them G sharps and this and that and everything, and brother, we had a time.

We finally kind of made it and we played the show, but I could mention this, this deal I was telling you about, the union thing that happened in Tulsa, well, this same band that they were having trouble about, the guy finally paid them but he had to get some more musicians and this man was angry (inaudible). So anyway, when I went out to my business agent, why did you let him put this on me and so and so, kidding he said, well, I don't know; and he had some pictures on the desk. I said let me have one of them pictures there and they guy said yes, autograph it and say, remember Coquille, Oregon. I said you better not, I'll shoot you, and he fell out.
That's the Mills Brothers?
Yeah, Mills Brothers. They said no, we're not going to do that, we'll say Chicago. I said that will be all right. So they said, one thing Ernie, you ought to have a (inaudible); In Coquille

you finally cleared it, but what they had up here with us, when we called a number, they never heard of it and they couldn't play it and they couldn't read and they said it was really murder but in Coquille you finally made it.
So you were the business agent, you went out to the club to collect the (inaudible)?
Yeah.
What was the name of the club?
Ziegfelds.
And the Mills Brothers came in all these years later and played?
Yeah; just last year.
Last year?
Yeah.
They remembered?
They remembered, they remembered when the man told them who it was, because we were so terrific all along in those theatres and they said forget about it.
(Inaudible). No, you couldn't but I continued going out and had all those dances there; they had to pay them too, they were under the musicians, but after all it cost and everything.

Usually now one guy--but you need more than just one man, I think Oscar Estelle was in the band, that's why we did finally make it and talking about Tulsa, you take Spurgeon, Earl Bostic, came up through high school under William Jett and they would always find the little bandstand out of the military band; then my brother came--the one that I was telling you when I first came out of school in Sand Springs, he moved into Tulsa and was a band director of high school, and really, Clarence Little was one guy that used to work on that little dance that they had. (Inaudible).
Oscar and Elon Watkins and I believe it was Thomas Ross, he's a trumpet player, he never did get to make it, he got into bad health, drinking, but was a very fine
musician--Thomas Ross--and he was a nice writer too. I think I have one of the old pictures that he was in.
One number was his--Thursday Evening Blues--that used to feature Artis Paul, a lot of high notes, was one of Thomas Ross'.
I knew him.
I think he went up in Dakota with Trent.
He came here with Nat Towles briefly too. I think he did some writing.
But he let the whiskey get him.
Now, the extent of your involvement in music now is union; you're the union delegate and you book?
Yes, I'm like the steward and I do booking also, because that's on my side for a little extra money, for the booking.
What do you think of the music of today as we know it? Just general-
ly speaking? Music as a whole today, as compared to the days when you were popular.

Well, frankly speaking, I think, believe it or not, we began to get--the music that we have as musicians to some extent is better, but I just don't believe or can't figure out how they're just for the dollar, but I think the promoters and operators is what's doing it. Everything is loud and amplification to turn down their mistakes; it's just so loud that you don't know. Like we were saying about those tenor men out of Dallas, you would look for what kind of tone somebody had, but now you may have a sorry tone and a good tone, you're not going to be able to tell what he's sticking in that mike and the way they go about it.

I think, to tell you the truth, a lot of that is going on in these rock and roll and disco joints, it'll run you crazy on it.
What do you think about

We have to accept it, that's it for today, but believe it or not, if you are closely related to the disco, it's fading some, and I'll tell you what they are doing now, a lot of times they're adding a little live along with it and I think in the long run, if we can stand it, then we will win out.
What do you think about the state of jazz, 1981?

Well, believe it or not, I never would have thought it, but I believe is beginning to come back. Why I say that, in my little booking, it's hard for jazz to get over in the small towns, well, in one way of speaking, Tulsa is even a small town compared to Omaha, well, I got a call a little before I left and he just pinpointed--he first wanted Eddie Harris, and he said I'm going to have this opening, I want to have a grand opening, I had some redecorating done and I want jazz, and I was just so surprised and I said

well, I don't know, I'll check around and see. I have done a little work for Eddie Harris but know if I can find him, he hasn't been in this area and he said what about Groove Holmes? Incidentally, I did know about Groove. Before I found Groove for him, Groove was supposed to open for him the first week in December.
Groove Holmes.

And so, in talking to him, he wanted something for in November and I mentioned several groups and one X rated group, which a lot of them are jumping after fast--what's the guy, Peter--but anyway, when I said something to him, he said no, no, I don't want that--
He wanted jazz?
Yeah; and I was glad, but I was surprised.
He stipulated Eddie Harris?
Yeah, yeah.
He's a great saxophone.
Yeah.
And I'll tell you another which he mentioned too, which is an oldtimer, Lou Rawls; he mentioned him, and he's been around a long time.

Do you think big bands as we knew them, because of course there are always going to be a few around, do you think big bands as we knew them will ever come back? Big bands, four trumpets, four trombones, five reeds and full rhythm section, like the Basie type of thing, do you think it will ever come back?
I don't believe it will in our day, but as the circle turns, I think it will because--but it's a question of where are they going to work.
And where's the money?
Yeah, that's it; because the way things are now, they just cost too much.
Too much for that many pieces. Just moving the band, transportation alone is prohibitive, and the salaries, hotel rent.

Now, when Basie goes which could be any day now, Basie's rather ill, he's seventy seven but he's not as youthful a seventy seven as you are. You're exactly seven days younger than Basie. Basie was born August 21, 1904; you were born August 28, 1904; one week difference.
I know we were close but I didn't know that close.
Physically you're in perfect shape, facially; everything. You look and act as if you were younger than Basie, because your health is good.
Basie was saying that too. I said him about six months ago, he was in Tulsa.
Now, when Basie goes, what's going to happen to that rich, charming,

black thing we had. And to pretend that there isn't a difference, there is a difference. Afro-American art is Afro-American art to a large extent, and the thing that Basie and Duke and Lundsford and all those had, and your band, was so unique; what's going to happen when Basie goes? This thing that Mercer, that Ellington is going around with, I don't consider.
No, and I don't know why, that even though he has a band, like I said this young man that came from my band, Minerve, the band is good, but it's some kind of way--
It's not Duke Ellington.
No, it's not.
He played Tulsa and it is pitiful.
He shouldn't say Duke Ellington.
Yeah.
It should simply say Mercer Ellington has a band, there is nothing about the great Duke; it is doing a disservice in my opinion, to Duke's memory.
I wonder and have thought a lot about it, and I even talked to Junior about it--
Your son?
Yeah.

He said Dad, it don't have a chance and I would say maybe if you got the proper backing and would go about it like the country and western that is popular today, well I mean throw a little of that in and he said, well, maybe but I kind of doubt it. The thing is who would have enough to invest that, that you could do it.
And sticking out the promotion until they build a name.
That's it.
How old is Ernie Fields Jr. now?
Junior is forty--he's in his forties--he's about forty-three.
I thought he was much younger than that.
No.
I didn't know, I thought he was--well, he was when he came to California.
Yeah, yeah, then, but that was several years ago.
Yeah, when I was still there.

Incidentally, right after this In The Mood, Rene discouraged me from using anything vocal there. It was still me, but what we did--I don't have any of that with me, but I'm going to send you a tape to send to Ron on (inaudible) and Ernie Fields Jr., because it would still mean that I produced that and I want you to see that. That was under his direction.
Is Ron writing about my life as a booker and this and that, because I did that
Did you ever attempt to sing like they advised you to?

I never did, not enough to call myself a singer, but I used to do Saints--believe it or not, I started to do that out in your place and I did Looking Back, and so Ernie has a joke he tells about me, which my sidekick is hunting and fishing and a young man is raising dogs in Tulsa has a dance hall also and I went in the ballroom one night and I had hunted with him and this and that, and when I said that I admired his dogs he said they were four and five hundred dollar dogs, you know, pups. So they all knew me in Tulsa and they announced me and said come on, do a number and so I went up and did the Saints Go Marching In. So the next day, the hunting date I had with the man, I went out hunting with him and he had a dog, oh, I just laughed like every-thing, and got to talking about it and I had a very high powered pointer then and this man

raised setters, and I said I have one setter but he's about seen his day, I sure would like to have a young setter. (Inaudible); he said the next time you come out and do a number for me, that's yours. So when we were going in, he said, I'm not kidding Ernie, but if you like it, sure enough, come around and see me again, and he gave me the dog.

So I came home and had it and Ernie was still around then and he came in and said oh, dad, you got one and I said yeah, a man gave me the dog. He gave you that dog? What did you pay for that dog? He said I know you love mama, and you're not henpecked, why don't you tell her, she don't mind you buying what you want. He said how in the world, all these years, you hired two vocalists and you come over there and a man gives you a dog for singing; and he really had me.
What key do you sing that in?
(Inaudible)
I did it at the convention with-- what's his name?
Charley Williamson.
Yeah; the piano player, who used to be our vice.
A black guy?
Yeah, black guy.
I don't know.
Yeah, you know, he used to come to your house you were saying, this piano player.
Come here?
No, he's not from here.
Oh, you mean national.
Yeah, he's one of the national officials.
He usually has a tempo band. It's Ernie Williamson, isn't it? He used to be the travelling delegate from National when we had the black local and everything.
Oh, oh, oh--
Ernie Lewis.
Lewis had a tempo band--
He used to stay with Basie Gibbons when he came here.

I want to ask you something about-- you know, so many of the singers today have become very famous and very popular and very successful, so they want to make a singer out of everyone, so a bandleader almost has to sing-- they want me to sing.
That's what Nat Cole tried to tell me.
Right. So the whole course of your life might have been different if you sang. How many of the famous singers can sing well? Very few of them.
Sure.
Some of them are terrible. The have some good promotion in front of them.
The whole course of your life,
Sure. Nat tried to tell me that when he said, I can't either, but he said I could and I did, and he said they wouldn't expect as much out of me; he said you would just learn whatever you could do.

Sometimes your very lack of ability is the thing that people like. It's just unique or different from the singers, guys like Dean Martin, he's not a great singer, but you become very popular. It's like a hit record, who cares how good a record is, as long as it sells.
However, In The Mood, was very well done.
After we saw this write up here, I got so many compliments on that.
This was November 8, 1941, Billboard, and it says: Reviewed at the

Rainbow Ballroom, Denver, Ernie Fields. Fields' engagement here was the first for a colored combination, other than for one-nighters and his week showing was one of the best the ballroom has had in several years. Music (inaudible) in that Fields kept on the swing side as well as the usual boogie. Library is extensive enough to cover both. Rene Hall takes care of the boogie arrangements while Gay Jones, the paleface, has been doing the sweet work. Guitar player doubles on trombone,--that would be Rene Hall--and Fields also takes a turn at the sliphorn to fill to seven brass. Carl is on bass now, Oklahoma City.
Where were you guys, in a nightclub somewhere sitting down?
Yeah. Count was playing somewhere that night and we said let's go out and catch Count, and so we did and he kind of came and sat a while.
This is in Orchestra World, June 1944; my goodness gracious.
After thirty nine, when I once appeared, of course Willard didn't
do much longer, but I still made those trips regularly, from east to west and if we didn't play anywhere else, we at least made that chain of the negro theatres that all the bands made.
There's Lawrence Welk right across from you in an article; and Lee Castle.
To tell you the truth, most likely the same man that was booking, before Lawrence got so big, Frederick Brothers was booking me about the same time they were booking Lawrence Welk.
Yeah, Frederick Brothers was booking you here on this flyer here.
Yeah, when I did the Rainbow Ballroom.
There you are, you were number--well, which poll was that?
Chicago--
Count Basie was number one, 30,000; Jimmy Lunsford, 27,000, Duke Ellington three, 21,000; Lionel Hampton, four,
20,000; Cab Calloway, five, 19,000; Erskine Hawkins, six, 18,000; Louis Armstrong, 17,000 and Ernie Fields, 16,000.

Well look at the bands below you. After you comes Earl Hines, Andy Kirk, Nobel Cecil, Les Hite, Ella Fitzgerald, John Kirby, Cecil Burke, Tiny Bradshaw, Swinging Rays, Claude Hopkins, Fats Waller, Adie South, Al Cooper--that would be the Savoy Sultans-- Coban Hawkins and Lucky Millinder.

Ernie, I think your marital life and your family life would make an interesting, long, protracted story, so why don't you just start out and tell us about your marriage, your wife's name is Bernice, the birth of your son Ernie, Jr., I know that was a big thing in your life, your daughter and the part they
played in the life of an orchestra man. That's a very special thing, people don't understand.
It definitely was, and she played a wonderful part. I guess from the beginning she began to understand.

I remember the first time I took my wife, I was playing the dance--they called it a food show, it was an advertisement and selling articles as frigidaires, icebox, this and that, cars and everything, and of course they had a band playing and free dancing, and I met my wife, a young lady named Ella Latimore was her name--
What was that?

Ella Latimore. A young lady who was a friend of my wife brought her and made me acquainted, and my wife, as I told you, attended Tuskegee Institute. My wife also did, but that was after my day, but Ella brought her around and I don't know what it was, but it just looked like something that impressed me and I don't know (inaudible), and
I said, my goodness, I've got to find out about this lady.

I met her that night and when the dance was over, and you know Preston, you've been in the business, I had to check up and everything and I had asked her when I met her could I take her home that night and both of them said yes.

I was a long time there and waited and it happened that Ella said Bernice wanted to leave, what in the world are you doing, the dance is over. I guess he was just trying to be nice and ask if he could take us home, so Ella told her, no I don't think Ernie would have said that if he didn't mean to; but I finally showed up (inaudible).

I took them home, I dropped Ella off and then went to her home, and when she got home, I didn't know anything about this, she told her mother who had brought her home, and she says, who are you talking about, Sonny Boy Fields?

She was born in Taft and I didn't know her, I'm about eight or nine years older than my wife, and so when they got through and we were acquainted and got back to her mother one time, and they all laughed and said, when she was born--like they go around and see little babies, I was with my mother and I looked and said, that sure is a pretty little baby.
And that turned out to be your wife?
That turned out to be my wife.
What was her maiden name?
Copeland. Bernice Copeland.
And she was born--
In Taft, Oklahoma. That's where I was raised, but I was born in Texas.
Her family moved away from Taft very soon, to Okmulgee. I'm trying to think
what young man was there--she mentioned after that some youngster went from Okmulgee and was very popular, outstanding, with Count's band sometime later. I don't remember his name, he played flute.
Anyway, she moved to Okmulgee and I didn't know anything about her after that.

We began to court and go around and of course I was on the road and some years later, I don't know, she just kind of let me know, we had been going around for about five years and in a nice way she let me know I'm tired of waiting and I always said I wanted to really have something, but she seemed to be very understanding, maybe we can get it together (inaudible). And so we got married.
In what year?
Approximately around 1936 or seven; somewhere along in there. We met several years before that. It may have been eight when we married.
We hadn't been married long when

this Hammond deal came; that was 1939. Again, she was very impressive when I went and talked to him about the contract and everything, and she said, you had the horn when I met you and I wish you luck, but whether it's good or bad you'll never have to say that I kept you from trying.

That's the way it went on and on. My travelling never did interfere, and I know like you might say these orchestra wives and everything, we'd be travelling and they'd would worry and a lot of them would worry about when they heard from them, have they done this, have they sent anything home.

Harry, who has known your wife, and of course I see what he's talking about, this is the first time I met her, I believe I did meet her somewhere just once before, but not to be around her like I am this time, and Harry said she sure is like your wife. I said what is that? She never meets a stranger. She don't care who it is and that's the way that
my wife is. Whoever is my friend, nobody particular, no class or no this or whatever, if that is my friend and they're good enough to be in my company, well they were all right with her.

We had a boy and a girl and a lot of my friends kid me and say undoubtedly I got Carmen by remote control. Carmen is, I think, about ten or twelve years younger than her brother, than Ernie Jr., and so anyway I started Ernie on the music very young and he did quite good; when he finished high school he got a scholarship, like football players and so on, athletes, but he got out of that real quick to go to Howard University, and I don't regret at all that it cost me.
(Inaudible)

after he began travelling, well I was proud that I had made the reputation that there wasn't anywhere that he went where he was ashamed to say that he was my son, and a lot of those promoters down south, all east and west, your dad played for me.
