A.G. Godley.
Yeah; that's it.

And later on when Godley left, Henry Smith, who was the father of Geechee Smith, and his home was in Tulsa and Trent broke up one of those times and so Henry Smith came back to Tulsa and so when he came back to Tulsa he would always--I always seemed to be doing more than any others down there and so I got Henry Smith in the band, and he was the greatest, a very fine drummer, and then we all predicted then his son, he began to play, we predicted he was going to turn out good, and he sure did. Geechee Smith turned out to be a very nice musician and he was one of those high note trumpet players.
Who was this white band that he found there--who was that guy Cherokee?
Charlie Barnet.
Yeah. I think he
worked with Charlie Barnet.
Yes, he did.

And of course, who would always be, as the years went on, right at the beginning, you had Earl Bostic and Luther West and they were all there and if anybody could compete with them, they were pretty darn good.
Earl, as far as a soloist, he was just tops.
Then we would come in, from Kansas City, those Douglas Brothers.
Gil, Buck and Tommy.
They were the epitome of the Kansas City style.
They were. It's just too bad that they didn't get on to the height that they should have.
Buck passed very young.
Then another young man--did you ever know Paul Quinichette?
We worked in our first band together, Lloyd Hunter band. We picked him up in Denver, 1941.
He was a tenor man in the band when I got there up in Chicago.
He imitated Lester Young..

I'll tell you another reason the Douglas Brothers didn't go further. Later Tommy played with Duke Ellington and Buck stayed in Chicago and Bill and I worked together with Nat Towles before he was drafted into the service. The reason they didn't go further is they had that great love for Kansas City, they didn't care to go anywhere. There was no need to go any further; Kansas City was a great jazz center then. It hasn't been in thirty something years.
That's the way it was with Elon Watkins. Elon, as I said, when Hamp raided my band and got Elon and Oscar Estelle--
Oscar died?
Yes.
In Tulsa?
Yes. Elon didn't stay with Hamp and I inquired later and Hamp said he was all right, he just came on back to Tulsa, you know, some of them just don't go for it.
I was always that way about Omaha.
Sure. So Elon came back and he's around Tulsa now.
Is that right?
Sure. He's playing now and then.

The other thing we might point out, in that day, there was a great reservoir of--a pool of musicians to select from. There were so many. Like in Omaha, there were hundreds of them, true great, improvisational jazz geniuses.
(Inaudible).
Nowadays they don't exist and the kids call themselves playing jazz and in many cases they are playing pure nonsense, just so called fusion and avant garde, and we're
That's it.
A man's ability doesn't change that much; you can either play or you can't. These guys walk around saying I play jazz; and they have no more conception of jazz than I would have of metaphysics.
It's really pitiful and it's frankly a disgrace to the profession.
It is.
Because somebody that knows, they wonder, nothing we can do about it, but they think that anybody shouldn't be able to sell that.

Our protests would be regarded as the ravings of some old men who are bitter; no, sir. You are very vital, anyone can tell that by talking to you, and I try to keep myself aware, I teach the history of jazz at the university and I have for five or six

years in a course called, Black Music (inaudible). Plus, as you know I'm a performer with young guys, I play with very young guys. It's just unfortunate that they don't want to be counselled and told. In many cases, some of the big names of jazz don't play well; they play badly. Why pretend otherwise? If that's your subjective opinion, why not say it? A guy's afraid to speak out because they'll say you're closeminded and narrowminded; that's not it. It's just that the standard has been lowered.

It is and then, I don't know, like you take Count, a very good friend of mine, and you know the ground he's covered, he knows, but if he can get somebody that just plays all right, because he may have two or three who can do the job, so, so what.
And he doesn't lead his own band, he sees very bad advice from management, we won't say any names, that guide his destiny, and Basie hasn't actively been a

leader for many years.
Basie's a very lonely man on his band stand after having played with Lester Young and Herschel and Doug Clayton and Harry Edison and Jack Washington. (Inaudible).
Jack died the same month as Sam Cooke. (Inaudible)
Basie is just going through the motions. The last time he was here in June, I introduced his band, I was paid to introduce him and present him with a painting that a fellow made, which I played with him in '45, '46, and '47, and it's a disgrace that he would take that band around the world today. I'm saying this is a disgrace that Mercer would take this band around and pass it off as Duke Ellington's band. But that's the way it is today.
Most of the guys in Basie's band-- we were very selective in our day, you could afford to be back in the forties and thirties. You know if you got a man in your band who
couldn't play, all the public would know it. Hey, that saxophone player is not with it; nowadays, who knows.
They don't care.
The whole thing has been corrupted by commercialization and the american dollar. We were fortunate enough to live in a great era of american music.
I wish you would speak to Ron and insist that he put this on the news media.
I'll address this to Ron and hope he gets it now. If Ron would send a news release--
Just of what you did.

In our newspaper--you see, I write a column for the paper, a weekly column, I didn't have one today because I was too busy to write it. I did one last week about the University of Iowa, doing a residency, but if Ron sent a news release (inaudible) to

my paper, The Omaha World Herald, they would print it and then I would get it on the syndicate. But it would be improper for me to write it because they would think I was building my own self up or build you up because you're my friend.
So I'll send Ron a letter to send a news release on this, for better or worse, assuming that we've done a great job. I sure hope we have.

I think that's all I have. You can get those pictures together and write a note on there, so he'll know what's what about them and then if he makes mention in his letter, he'll register them and put on there to make copies and return them.
Well, at 5:07, Sunday, November 1, 1981, Ernie Fields and I, Preston Love, will sign off.
(Whereupon, interview is completed and transcript is concluded.)

segments.chapter: Childhood in Taft and Muskogee
segments.title: Copyright notice, title page and opening of the interview
segments.summary: Rutgers copyright notice and title page for the NEA Jazz Oral History interview of Ernie Fields by Preston Love, October 31, 1981; Love introduces Fields as the Tulsa-based southwest bandleader.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Taft and Muskogee
segments.title: Birth in Nacogdoches, move to Taft, and being named Ernie Lawrence Fields
segments.summary: Fields gives his birth date, parents, his father's death in 1906, and how he went by Sonny Boy until he named himself.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Taft and Muskogee
segments.title: Growing up poor but sheltered in an all-black Oklahoma town
segments.summary: As the baby of a musical family he never knew hard times, though his widowed mother farmed; his sisters played piano and brothers sang; he walked miles to hear country picnic music.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Taft and Muskogee
segments.title: Taking up piano and dreaming of baseball
segments.summary: His sister urges him to learn music and he starts piano, but his dream is big-league baseball even though he cannot run.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Taft and Muskogee
segments.title: Eva Jessye, his first real music teacher
segments.summary: Eva Jessye teaches him piano and voice in Taft, later becomes Dr. Eva Jessye with her own choir, and visits him at the Apollo.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Taft and Muskogee
segments.title: Wanting to be a mechanic and choosing Tuskegee
segments.summary: He dreams of baseball and auto mechanics, hears one can work one's way through Tuskegee, and ends up studying applied electricity; his brother, a Tuskegee band trumpeter, kids him.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Taft and Muskogee
segments.title: Working as a section-gang water boy to save for Tuskegee
segments.summary: He badgers the railroad foreman Roy Martin into a water-boy job and saves money, planning to go to Tuskegee.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Taft and Muskogee
segments.title: Shining shoes in Muskogee and befriending Walter Thomas
segments.summary: In a Muskogee shine parlor he learns the trade's ways with help from Walter Thomas, who is saving for the Kansas Vocational School.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Taft and Muskogee
segments.title: Dishwashing at Bishop's Cafe in Tulsa
segments.summary: Summer job washing dishes in a big Tulsa cafe while his mother stays with his brother in Sand Springs.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Taft and Muskogee
segments.title: The Tulsa race riot and his mother's worry
segments.summary: Fields explains that he went to Tulsa after the big riot, either 1917 or 1918 by his guess, and his mother worried.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Taft and Muskogee
segments.title: Hearing a white orchestra at Bishop's Cafe
segments.summary: Helping the busboy so he can hang around the dining room, he hears his first real orchestra with violins and horns.

segments.chapter: Tuskegee Institute
segments.title: Registering at Tuskegee and the Oklahoma reputation
segments.summary: At the registrar's office he is warned about his Oklahoma predecessors, including his brother Clarence Fields and Jake Simmons, and meets some careless Oklahoma natives.

segments.chapter: Tuskegee Institute
segments.title: Buying a three-dollar trombone and joining the Tuskegee second band
segments.summary: Hearing the Tuskegee band makes him want a horn; Owens finds him a trombone and Captain Frank Dryer has it repaired and puts him in the second band.

segments.chapter: Tuskegee Institute
segments.title: Learning trombone with William Moore at the power plant
segments.summary: Studying applied electricity, he works summer shifts at the power plant with clarinetist William Moore, who drills him on music, and Captain Dryer rewards him with a new Conn trombone.

segments.chapter: Tuskegee Institute
segments.title: Tuskegee student group and rivalry with Erskine Hawkins
segments.summary: He and fellow students, including a Stevenson, try to form a group to outdo Erskine Hawkins' band at Alabama State.

segments.chapter: Tuskegee Institute
segments.title: Suspended for pressing his uniform in his room
segments.summary: Caught ironing by the ROTC captain Stock, the electrician is suspended for a week and has to find lodging off campus.

segments.chapter: Tuskegee Institute
segments.title: Girlfriends Agnew Findlay and Blanche Franklin, the officers' ball and band trips
segments.summary: He stays with Steve, then drifts from Agnew Findlay to Blanche Franklin; the band wins warrant-officer status for the officers' ball and travels to games where Hawkins' band plays.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: Back in Sand Springs helping his brother's Pythian band
segments.summary: After graduating he returns to Sand Springs, where his trumpeter brother leads a Knights of Pythias band and lets him conduct the marching band.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: Wiring a duplex and working for Spot and Tate Electric
segments.summary: He wires a duplex without a license, a Black electrical contractor firm inspects it and hires him; the tape side ends.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: First gigs in Tulsa with William Ball and T.D. Thomas
segments.summary: He picks up gigs with William Ball and pianist T.D. Thomas, and during a trouble call hears a high school group in the Royal Annex Hall.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: Auditioning for Eddie Heywood Sr. with Butterbeans and Susie
segments.summary: Heywood Sr. needs a trombone for the TOBA show at the Dixie Theatre; Fields reads the book, the band tests him with a jam, and Heywood hires him.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: Eddie Heywood Jr. and the autographed picture
segments.summary: Fields later met Heywood Jr., who played the Apollo and Royal with his band, and recalls Marshal Royal playing in Heywood's combo.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: Declining to go on the road with Butterbeans and Susie
segments.summary: Though he worked the whole season, he turned down touring with vaudeville shows, recalling how Basie got stranded.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: Foots Thomas and the Missourians job he turned down
segments.summary: Walter 'Foots' Thomas, now with the Missourians, offers to get him a fifty-dollar-a-week job, but Fields stays in Tulsa.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: Taking over the high-school boys' band with Roy Milton and Eddie Nicholson
segments.summary: The group with Roy Milton and Roy Randall makes Fields leader; he again turns down Foots' Cab Calloway offer, tours Kansas, and hires Eddie Nicholson on drums.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: Dating his early band, around 1927
segments.summary: Love works out the date from Fields' age; Fields praises Eddie Nicholson's drumming.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: Phil Dorsey, Ponca City, and arranger Dave Duncan
segments.summary: Promoter Phil Dorsey steers work to the band; in Ponca City trombonist Dave Duncan offers arrangements, and a call comes from the east Texas oil boom.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: How the taxi dance worked
segments.summary: Fields explains the ten-cents-a-dance system and paying bands on percentage.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: The Gladewater and Longview oil-boom gig
segments.summary: The band plays a ballroom between the two east Texas oil towns for a white manager, in mud and rain, with money borrowed from his brother.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: Personnel of the Gladewater band and Luther 'Spurgeons' West
segments.summary: Fields names Luther West, Roy Milton, Eddie Nicholson, Cecil Smith, Roy Walker, Pete Bailey; Love recalls hearing West with Fields in 1941.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: Bounced checks and a Texas Ranger slapping Pete Bailey
segments.summary: The manager's checks bounce, a Ranger strikes Pete Bailey, and the band forces the man to pay them something.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: Sugar Lou and Eddie, a Tyler brother-sister act
segments.summary: Fields recalls the popular east Texas group of Sugar Lou and Eddie, brother and sister from Tyler.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: Alphonso Trent's band in Tulsa and its young players
segments.summary: Seeing Trent's band in Tulsa inspired him to form a big band; Trent had Lee Hilliard and Leslie Sheffield, whom Love later worked with.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: T. Holder at the Louvre Ballroom in Tulsa
segments.summary: T. Holder's band plays taxi dances at the Louvre, later renamed Kane's Ballroom; Love notes Holder and Trent as great southwest bands.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: Learning from T. Holder's closed rehearsals
segments.summary: Holder lets Fields sit in on closed rehearsals and lectures his men to cover for a soloist's mistakes.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: Holder's gambling and the band voting Andy Kirk in as leader
segments.summary: Holder gambles away the band's pay; the owner Faulkenberg tells the men to take over the business, and they vote Andy Kirk to run it.

segments.chapter: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
segments.title: Kirk's offer, and knowing Holder and Trent only informally
segments.summary: Kirk replaces pianist Jack with Mary Lou and asks Fields about joining; Fields never played regularly with Holder, Kirk or Trent, though he later played for Trent in Fort Smith.

segments.chapter: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
segments.title: Dave Duncan joins as arranger and lives in the Fields home
segments.summary: Fields hires the white arranger Dave Duncan, and his mother worries about neighbours when Duncan boards at their house.

segments.chapter: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
segments.title: Dorsey books the Denver battle of bands against Smiling Billy Stewart
segments.summary: Phil Dorsey lines up small-town dates and a winner-take-all battle of bands in Colorado; Fields dates it about 1930-32 and talks about a white man in a Black band.

segments.chapter: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
segments.title: Dave Duncan fits in; Grant Williams joins; the Louvre Ballroom
segments.summary: Duncan wins the band over, guitarist Grant Williams joins, and Fields explains the all-white Louvre Ballroom where Fletcher Henderson played a week.

segments.chapter: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
segments.title: The Tulsa Club hires a Black band for the first time
segments.summary: A head waiter pushes Fields' seven-piece band into the exclusive Tulsa Club for a week, including the Skelly daughter's party, a first for Tulsa.

segments.chapter: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
segments.title: Quitting the electric shop to go to Denver
segments.summary: Fields tells his bosses he may not return and the band agrees to go to Denver.

segments.chapter: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
segments.title: The Denver band's personnel, including Herbert Scott from Bessie Smith's band
segments.summary: Roy Milton sings, and Herbert Scott, lately of Bessie Smith's band, plays trumpet with Hobart Banks, West and Nicholson.

segments.chapter: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
segments.title: The battle of the bands against Smiling Billy Stewart's Sarasota Serenaders
segments.summary: The two bands play at opposite ends of the hall; Roy Milton's vocal on I'll Always Be In Love With You wins the crowd, but Stewart's big band from Florida is stronger and Fields resolves to enlarge his band.

segments.chapter: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
segments.title: Denver promoter Jones and the Rosonia ballroom
segments.summary: The promoter Jones likes the band and promises return dates at the ballroom.

segments.chapter: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
segments.title: Earl Bostic, Tulsa High School and the broken clarinet
segments.summary: Band director William Jett gives young Earl Bostic a clarinet, which Bostic's junk-dealer father breaks; Fields also notes Bostic subbing for Luther West.

segments.chapter: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
segments.title: Bostic and West at college, Luther West's draft, and the Catholic teacher Freeman
segments.summary: Bostic at Creighton, West at Xavier, West's induction and Love's 1943 call from Fields; Mr. Freeman taught both boys.

segments.chapter: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
segments.title: Recruiting Rene Hall and the Biloxi Golden Gloves story
segments.summary: West brings Rene Hall from New Orleans; his mother consents after Rene's close call with a white mob at a Golden Gloves bout.

segments.chapter: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
segments.title: Rene Hall's warnings about the deep South and the arranging-for-trombone deal
segments.summary: Rene warns Fields that the deep South differs from Oklahoma; they agree he will teach Fields arranging for lessons in guitar.

segments.chapter: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
segments.title: Walter Pichon, the arranger who forgot to book gigs
segments.summary: Rene tells of Walter Pichon in New Orleans, so absorbed in music that he lined up no work after a Memphis hotel engagement; Fields still has his arrangement of Stardust.

segments.chapter: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
segments.title: Rene Hall practising trombone, leaving, and staying a best friend
segments.summary: Rene practises trombone late at night, buys his own horn, leaves for Earl Hines, and remains Fields' closest friend.

segments.chapter: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
segments.title: Leaving the electric job and the Schoonover tour of the northwest
segments.summary: Back at the Tulsa Club story, Fields quits electric work, adds players, and signs with agent H.E. Schoonover for a northwest tour.

segments.chapter: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
segments.title: Travelling in two cars and the New Mexico commercial permit
segments.summary: With instruments on the car roofs, the band is stopped at a port of entry and made to buy a twenty-five-dollar permit.

segments.chapter: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
segments.title: Hiring Salva Sanders, Count Basie's early idol
segments.summary: Salva Sanders quits the Southern Serenaders after their pianist falls off the stool drunk, and Fields takes him on.

segments.chapter: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
segments.title: Roy Milton and Roy Walker leave for California
segments.summary: Roy Milton, Roy Walker and drummer Samson Pratt head to California, so Fields needs a vocalist.

segments.chapter: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
segments.title: Pee Wee Wiley, later Reverend Wiley
segments.summary: Vocalist Pee Wee Wiley joins after the Texas Rangers band, and years later is assistant pastor in Watts.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: Melvin Moore first appears with Don Albert's band
segments.summary: In Tulsa with Don Albert, young Melvin Moore says he will join Fields' band once he finishes high school in Oklahoma City.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: Salva Sanders as a blues player and the western tours
segments.summary: With the enlarged band Schoonover books a tour west; Salva Sanders keeps conservative habits and plays strong blues.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: Salva Sanders' illness and death
segments.summary: On the northwest tour Salva wins at cards and eats little, then sickens and dies around 1936-37, probably of cancer.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: Melvin Moore, the great vocalist
segments.summary: Fields praises Moore as greater than Ella Fitzgerald, with a voice for scat, blues and ballads, who recorded for Vocalion, and regrets the band did not push him.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: T Town Blues, the 1980 tribute and the 1939 Hammond sessions
segments.summary: A singer revives T Town Blues the night Count Basie honours Fields in Tulsa; the 1939 Hammond sessions did not get the push they deserved.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: First trip to the Apollo and Willard Alexander's plan
segments.summary: Love saw Melvin at the Apollo; Fields explains Alexander planned to leave William Morris and Basie asks why he would go back to Tulsa.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: Stolen uniforms and Ella Fitzgerald taking the Savoy slot
segments.summary: His uniforms are stolen from the car before the Apollo, Alexander pays for new suits, and the Savoy broadcast spot goes to Ella Fitzgerald after Chick Webb's death.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: Russell 'Big Chief' Moore auditions in New York
segments.summary: Trombonist Russell Moore, an Indian from Omaha, auditions at the Woodside Hotel and is sensational.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: Basie advises Fields not to go home
segments.summary: Basie tells Fields Alexander will look out for him and not to return to Oklahoma.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: The band's loyalty and Rozelle Claxton's ultimatum
segments.summary: The men say they will follow him back home; Rozelle Claxton says he will take Eddie South's offer if the band leaves.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: Heading back with dates arranged by Alexander and Walter Barnes
segments.summary: Alexander gets Philadelphia and other dates, an old contact books Chicago, and Claxton leaves.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: Hobart Banks rejoins at a Longbell dance hall
segments.summary: Back in Oklahoma Fields books western-swing barns with help from Bob Wills; the men joke about Hobart hitchhiking to the job.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: How John Hammond tracked Fields down in Tulsa
segments.summary: Hammond, after hearing of Fields in Kansas City, calls through a waiter at the Club Lido; Fields' wife relays the message after Hammond tips the waiter five dollars.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: Auditioning for Hammond at the Crystal Palace
segments.summary: Fields plays for Hammond at Walter Tate's Crystal Palace and arranges for Hammond and Alexander to hear the band in Wichita.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: Melvin Moore doubts it was really John Hammond
segments.summary: Melvin thinks Hammond with a hole in his trousers could not be the millionaire.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: Hammond and Alexander arrive at the Wichita dance
segments.summary: They slip in unseen and approach at intermission, delighted with the program.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: Hammond's caution about contracts and the drummer Clarence Dickson
segments.summary: Hammond asks whether any member cannot be fired and says Joe Jones had spoiled him on drummers, while Fields' Clarence Dickson is lighter.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: Basie's hotel opening and Alexander's contract offer
segments.summary: At Basie's opening without Joe Keyes, Fields learns the value of reliable players; Alexander offers a contract and Hammond promises to record him.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: Hobart Banks stays home; Rozelle Claxton replaces him
segments.summary: Hobart will not leave his family for five years, so Fields hires Claxton through the Kansas City union.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: The trumpet section and the slow reader Amos Woodruff
segments.summary: Press calls Fields a cross between Duke and the Count; Amos Woodruff is a fine soloist but reads slowly, while Jeff Carrington and the Milton twins share first trumpet.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: Firing Amos Woodruff and Alexander's reaction
segments.summary: Fields lets Amos go to please his section and Rene Hall, then Alexander on the phone is aghast.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: Hiring Amos back and his solos on T Town Blues
segments.summary: Hammond wanted the southwest feel, so Fields rehires Amos, whose solos made T Town Blues a hit.

segments.chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
segments.title: Hammond wanted Hobart Banks for Benny Goodman
segments.summary: Hammond tells Fields he would have given him five thousand dollars for Hobart to replace Teddy Wilson, and later sent Hobart to Cafe Society.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: The old Jack Crawford bus
segments.summary: He buys a used stagecoach-style bus Jack Crawford had traded in, and later a new blue-and-white school bus.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: Crashing into moonshiners in Henryetta
segments.summary: Driving past a no-Negroes town, he rear-ends a car of moonshiners and the police take his side.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: The southwest tenor sound
segments.summary: Love asks about the southwest tenor sound; Fields says all had a big tone and swing, naming Bert Jones, Hal Singer, Jacquet and Arnett Cobb.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: The Houston battle against Milton Larkin, promoted by Don Robey
segments.summary: Don Robey invites Fields to Houston to play beside Milton Larkin's band with Cobb and Jacquet; Fields mentions Fred Beckett and wanting Tadd Dameron to arrange.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: Rene Hall's New York trips and the Bill Robinson tour
segments.summary: Rene went on several New York trips, and a 1943-44 write-up covers the tour with Bill Robinson.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: Melvin Moore's accident, loyalty and later jobs
segments.summary: Kenton admires Melvin; after a fall from a ladder he stays loyal, later working with Millinder and Dizzy Gillespie, and losing the Elliot Lawrence tour.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: The bus breaks down in Lee County, Florida
segments.summary: After mentioning Chris Goddard of London, Fields tells of a water pump failing in Florida and eating at a roadside cafe.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: Ordered out of town in fifteen minutes
segments.summary: A white man gives the band fifteen minutes to leave; Melvin has them push the bus down the road.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: Passing Black motorists refuse to tow; a white farmer does
segments.summary: Black drivers with wood slow past for fear; a white man with a boy tows them to a garage and refuses pay.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: The colored hotel and Lee County's reputation
segments.summary: At the next town, locals say Lee County is one of the worst in the state, citing a Black prisoner shot by deputies.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: Harold Iller, the white replacement for Luther West
segments.summary: Fields hires white Harold Iller from Minneapolis after Luther West is inducted, at the Happy Hour, from where he called Love.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: Jacksonville police threaten the band at the train station
segments.summary: A policeman tells tenor man Muse that band is no job for a Black man; Fields shelters the band on railroad property, and Jay McShann's band was arrested there later.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: Miami: Russell Embray shoved, and Iller barred from the Black cab
segments.summary: Lead trumpeter Embray is pushed off the sidewalk and white band manager Iller has trouble riding to the Black hotel and the Esquire Club.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: The union agent and the policeman who called Iller a creole
segments.summary: Parker Berry's worry about a mixed band is realised when the union agent and officer question Iller, and Fields settles it by saying he looks white but is creole.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: Sidemen who passed through the band: Geesil Minerve and Harold Bruce
segments.summary: Fields lists players who went on to big bands, such as Geesil Minerve and Harold Bruce.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: Leslie Sheffield, the Pittsfield booking and Rudy Morrison
segments.summary: Sheffield, formerly of Trent's band, helped set up Fields' Pittsfield tour; Rudy Morrison later went to Billy Eckstine.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: A gas stop near Shreveport and the sandwich shop
segments.summary: After filling up in Longview and Shreveport, Fields describes his band's members and how Warren Luckey and Carl White went for sandwiches.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: White men attack Warren Luckey and Fields is hit with a tire tool
segments.summary: A crowd follows the two musicians out; Luckey fights back, and Fields, trying to intervene, is struck, until a station owner threatens the attackers.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: Doctor's visit and the dance at Foxdale
segments.summary: The station owner will not call police; Fields is treated at a doctor's office and later x-rayed in Tulsa.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: Loose wheel lugs in Alva and the helpful young man
segments.summary: Only the only time he was in jail begins with a bus with two wheel lugs; a young fan persuades his father to send a mechanic at 2 A.M.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: The young man's happiest moment
segments.summary: The student, studying agriculture in Wichita, says working with a Black classmate changed his mind about his family's views.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: A night in the Enid jail with the Black policeman Tom
segments.summary: Arriving in Enid at dawn, Fields and Rene Hall sleep in jail cells while the others stay in the bus.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: Breakfast in the kitchen annex and hunting quail with promoter Dewey Goosby
segments.summary: Segregated meals in Enid, then friendship with promoter Dewey Goosby who takes him quail hunting; dated about 1936-37.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: Touring the northwest for Pops McElroy
segments.summary: During the war Goosby is in the Portland shipyards; Fields tours there under Pops McElroy's ballroom bookings.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: Dewey Goosby calls him off the bandstand
segments.summary: Goosby calls pretending to be Fields' wife, complaining that Black patrons are not being admitted to the white dance.

segments.chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
segments.title: Getting Goosby's party into McElroy's ballroom
segments.summary: Fields advises Goosby on how to demand admission, and Pops McElroy admits his party free.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: Bill Evans (Yusef Lateef) and the trumpeter Julius Watkins
segments.summary: Love lists famous saxophonists from the band; Fields says Bill Evans recommended Julius Watkins, who doubled on french horn.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: Leroy Cooper, the underrated baritone and lead saxophonist
segments.summary: Cooper later directed Ray Charles' band; Fields praises his willingness to play whatever dance music the crowd wanted.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: The Regal session Rene Hall arranged in New Jersey, with Cooper and Chambers
segments.summary: Fields pays for a bootleg union session in Jersey; the record featuring Cooper on baritone later turns up as a hit in Europe.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: Publishing: Teddy McRae and the 1939 Jubilee Swing royalty
segments.summary: Hammond's circle teach him to publish his own tunes, and in 1981 he gets a small London royalty for Jubilee Swing.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: Booker Ervin from Denison, Texas
segments.summary: On Buster Smith's tip he hires Booker Ervin, a big-toned Dallas-style tenor who stayed a couple of years.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: Don Byas of Muskogee
segments.summary: Fields foresaw Byas' success; Love recalls rooming with him in Basie's band in 1943 and his later life in Europe.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: Candy Johnson
segments.summary: Fields hired Candy Johnson in Ohio for a tour before he joined Basie.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: Hiring Jack Scott and Teddy Edwards from Mississippi
segments.summary: Fields signs guitarist Jack Scott and his friend Teddy Edwards, whom he puts in charge of the reed section.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: Yusef Lateef as Bill Evans: praying toward the sun on the bus
segments.summary: Evans, studying Muslim ideas, asks the bus to stop at five o'clock to face the sun.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: Artis Paul, the high-note trumpet player
segments.summary: Artis Paul, from Texas and a friend of Hot Lips Page, impressed Stan Kenton but drank and moved between Fields and Nat Towles.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: Russell 'Chief' Moore, four years in the band
segments.summary: Fields visited Moore in New York in 1980; he calls him one of the finest trombonists.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: Why musicians revered Fields, and the white players Eli Wilinsky and Harold Iller
segments.summary: Love says every sideman respected him; Fields recalls a mixed band in 1928 before Benny Goodman, and Iller's chair.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: Fields' bandleading philosophy: the band is the show
segments.summary: He never pushed himself as soloist, featured his men and learned from T. Holder that nobody is better than the person beside them.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: Leon Wright's showmanship, the dress act and Flip Wilson
segments.summary: Wright steals saxophone battles with Bill Evans and does a dress comedy act with Geesil Minerve that he says Flip Wilson copied.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: The Tougaloo dentist and Sammy Edwards' toothache
segments.summary: A white dentist pulls drummer Sammy Edwards' tooth on his porch so no white patient will see a Black man in his chair.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: Leon Wright's earring and 'me no savvy'
segments.summary: Wright gets served by pretending not to speak English.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: Boys at a general store think Ernie Fields must be a town up north
segments.summary: Black youths paying at the counter see the bus sign and assume Ernie Fields is a northern town.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: Life on the bus; Fields' dislike of gambling
segments.summary: Cards and dice passed the time but Fields avoided gambling, after seeing it ruin T. Holder.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: Clarice Ford and the violent trumpeter Deek Wilson
segments.summary: The dancer Clarice Ford's jealous boyfriend Deek Wilson fights anyone who smiles at her; Fields once fired a pistol over his head, yet they stayed friends.

segments.chapter: Sidemen, saxophonists and band life
segments.title: Fair treatment of sidemen; Basie Gibbens remembers
segments.summary: He never had violence with his men; Basie Gibbens recalls that men said Fields was fair.

segments.chapter: Local 94, Local 808 and the union convention
segments.title: Attending the national union convention and the union's weakness
segments.summary: He meets Gibbens at union conventions and thinks the union is getting weak and says he pushed a by-law.

segments.chapter: Local 94, Local 808 and the union convention
segments.title: Tony Twist's lawsuit against Zigfields and the Local 94 by-law
segments.summary: After Local 94 had to fight Zigfields in court, Fields wins a by-law for civil suits at the local's expense.

segments.chapter: Local 94, Local 808 and the union convention
segments.title: Joining Dallas Local 168 and founding Tulsa's Black Local 808
segments.summary: Black musicians could not join the white Tulsa local, so Fields joined Dallas 168, then helped found Local 808, later merged into 94.

segments.chapter: Local 94, Local 808 and the union convention
segments.title: Going as a delegate to the Hawaii convention
segments.summary: Substituting for an ill vice president, he is shown a resolution requiring merged locals to send a Black delegate.

segments.chapter: Local 94, Local 808 and the union convention
segments.title: Lining up speakers and the secretary's objection
segments.summary: Fields talks to speakers before the session; his own secretary worries the resolution will invite other groups' demands.

segments.chapter: Local 94, Local 808 and the union convention
segments.title: Speaking at mike seven and passing the resolution
segments.summary: He speaks for the Black delegate resolution and the hall stands unanimously, except one man from Florida.

segments.chapter: Local 94, Local 808 and the union convention
segments.title: Weak unions in small towns, and Marvin Young the lawyer and arranger
segments.summary: Love and Fields agree unions are weak outside the big cities; Fields tells how he gave Marvin Young an arrangement and Young became a fine arranger.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: J.J. Johnson joins the band and writes arrangements
segments.summary: Recommended by Clarence Little of the Ferguson Brothers agency, J.J. Johnson briefly joins Fields in New York and gives him arrangements.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: Charlie Williamson, and photos of Plas Johnson, Earl Palmer, Rene Hall and Ernie Jr.
segments.summary: Love remembers Charlie Williamson, a King Oliver trumpeter and union authority, then shows a photo of the 1958 session and asks Fields to tell the In The Mood story.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: Rene Hall comes to Dallas to arrange between Earl Hines jobs
segments.summary: When Earl Hines is idle, Fields sends for Rene Hall to arrange for him in Dallas in the 1940s.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: Ernie Jr.'s schooling, Howard University, and turning to music
segments.summary: Fields did not want his son to be a musician; Junior studies clarinet, goes to Texas College and Howard, and finally majors in music.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: Planning a Los Angeles session and taping the band in Seattle
segments.summary: Rene says he can get a session; Fields has a hobbyist record the band in stereo in Seattle in 1958 and sends the tape.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: Rene Hall hears the stereo tape and urges instrumentals
segments.summary: Played in mono, the tape sounds wrong; once heard properly Rene loves it, and he urges Fields to record instrumentals rather than vocals.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: The Williams Air Force Base cafe incident
segments.summary: Refused service at an Arizona all-night cafe, trumpeter Wallace Wilson and a white serviceman threaten to tear the place up.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: Firing Artis Paul in Las Vegas and the union hearing
segments.summary: Fields pays off drunk Artis Paul rather than use him in Las Vegas; Artis files charges and then confirms Fields' account.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: Returning to the coast with Hunter Gray and Butch Luckett
segments.summary: Back on the west coast, West is absent, so Hunter 'Shoe Sole' Gray and Butch Luckett fill in.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: The Frisco label and Fields' earlier records
segments.summary: Fields recorded Butches Blues on his own Frisco label, with a Golden Gate Bridge design, before the national success of In The Mood.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: The drunken Hollywood session with Butch Luckett and Hunter Gray
segments.summary: Rene brings in replacements, but the musicians turn up drunk, and the session yields only a few weak sides such as Strolling After School.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: Rene Hall, Earl Palmer and Rod Pierce set up Rendezvous sessions
segments.summary: Hall, Palmer and others plan sessions under Fields' name and sell the idea to producer Rod Pierce of Rendezvous.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: Recording In The Mood and Christopher Columbus; the trade reviews
segments.summary: Fields reads the July 1959 Cash Box review of Rendezvous 110, with Love noting composer Joe Garland and explaining the backing vocals.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: Flipping the record: In The Mood becomes the A side
segments.summary: An Oklahoma City DJ suggests flipping the record; Pierce agrees and In The Mood takes off.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: Twenty-three weeks on the charts, American Bandstand and the money
segments.summary: The hit led to Dick Clark's show; the money was split among corporation and players, though appearances paid well.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: Joe Garland's saxophone exercise and Louis Armstrong's refusal
segments.summary: Love explains that Garland wrote In The Mood as an exercise; Armstrong would not touch it, and Plas Johnson's tenor on the rock version is praised.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: Chattanooga Choo Choo and Capitol's offer for the contract
segments.summary: After a second Rendezvous session, Capitol offers to buy the contract; Fields holds out for fifty thousand and ends up signing without payment.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: The 1964 Capitol Swanee River session
segments.summary: Love reads the Billboard notice of the 1964 Capitol single; the session did nothing.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: Nat King Cole, the trio, and singing
segments.summary: Fields toured with Nat Cole, who told him he too had once said he could not sing; Parker Berry doubted Cole could be a vocalist.

segments.chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
segments.title: Nat Cole answers the question about jazz in Denver
segments.summary: A young man asks Cole why he doesn't play jazz and Cole jokes about his beaver cap and tinted glasses.

segments.chapter: Booking agents and Harry Burns
segments.title: Pittsburgh Courier clippings: third among bands in 1952
segments.summary: Love reads Courier write-ups ranking Fields third behind Duke and Basie in 1952.

segments.chapter: Booking agents and Harry Burns
segments.title: Bill Robinson tour, Estelle Edson and Marl Young
segments.summary: Love goes through a programme of the Bo Jangles tour and Fields remembers singer Estelle Edson and her friendship with Marl Young.

segments.chapter: Booking agents and Harry Burns
segments.title: Booking agencies after Alexander, and Helen Humes
segments.summary: Fields lists the agencies that booked him, including Joe Artis and the Ferguson Brothers, and a tour with Helen Humes.

segments.chapter: Booking agents and Harry Burns
segments.title: How Harry Burns of New Orleans began booking the band
segments.summary: In McAlester, Oklahoma, agent Harry Burns, born Bernstein, meets Fields and books three or four dates.

segments.chapter: Booking agents and Harry Burns
segments.title: Lake Charles: a man with a forty-five orders the dance to continue
segments.summary: When Fields ends the dance, a man draws a pistol and demands more music; the doorman defuses it, proving Rene Hall's warnings.

segments.chapter: Booking agents and Harry Burns
segments.title: Burns' tours collapse in Kentucky
segments.summary: Burns' later bookings dry up, the cars break down in Kentucky and the band returns to Tulsa broke.

segments.chapter: Booking agents and Harry Burns
segments.title: Demanding contracts and a deposit, and buying a used Flexible bus
segments.summary: Burns wants him for an Easter opening in Miami; Fields insists on six weeks of contracts and uses them to buy a bus on credit.

segments.chapter: Booking agents and Harry Burns
segments.title: The Miami and Fort Lauderdale garnishee over a contract clause
segments.summary: A hidden clause barred playing Fort Lauderdale near Miami; a deputy tries to tie up his money and bus, but a lawyer says the bus cannot be seized.

segments.chapter: Booking agents and Harry Burns
segments.title: Playing a dance on a floor that was not there
segments.summary: Burns' bookings sometimes went wrong; one venue had no piano and no dance floor.

segments.chapter: Booking agents and Harry Burns
segments.title: Playing the University of Miami homecoming, a first for a Black band
segments.summary: Burns persuades Miami students to fly the band in for homecoming; Fields shows a photo with Dr. Thurston Adams.

segments.chapter: Booking agents and Harry Burns
segments.title: Burns taking bank deposits for dates Fields did not know about
segments.summary: Burns collects money from military bases for return dates Fields never contracted, and the FBI moves in.

segments.chapter: Booking agents and Harry Burns
segments.title: The FBI looking for Harry Burns in Vernal, Utah
segments.summary: Singer Al Harris joins the band in Utah and is grilled by an agent about Burns, whom Fields never finds again.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Playing the Apollo regularly 1939-50 and the theatre circuit
segments.summary: Fields appeared at the Apollo nearly every year, where he gathered sidemen like Gene Ammons, Wallace Wilks and Bill Evans.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Working with the Mills Brothers and the Coquille, Oregon story
segments.summary: He backed the Mills Brothers in the East and in Oregon, where the Mills Brothers' mocking autograph jokes recall a Tulsa union dispute.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Tulsa musicians: Oscar Estelle, Elon Watkins and Thomas Ross
segments.summary: Tulsa's high-school band tradition produced West and Bostic; Fields remembers trumpeter-writer Thomas Ross, who wrote Thursday Evening Blues.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: His present work as union steward and booker; music today
segments.summary: Fields now serves as union steward and books bands; he finds modern music too loud, amplified and disco-dominated.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: The state of jazz in 1981
segments.summary: He thinks jazz is returning, as a Tulsa club owner asked for jazz acts such as Eddie Harris, Groove Holmes and Lou Rawls.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Will big bands come back?
segments.summary: Both doubt big bands will return in their day because of costs.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: When Basie goes: Mercer Ellington's band and the Black big-band tradition
segments.summary: Fields and Love, comparing ages with Basie, worry that the Afro-American big band spirit will die and criticise Mercer Ellington's band for using Duke's name.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Ernie Jr.'s age, and Rene Hall's guidance after In The Mood
segments.summary: Fields notes Junior is about forty-three and that Rene discouraged vocals on the post-hit records.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Singing The Saints and winning a setter dog
segments.summary: He sang for a dog-breeder friend and was given a setter, which his son teases him about.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Misremembered union official Charley Williamson, Ernie Williamson or Ernie Lewis
segments.summary: Fields and Love try to work out the name of the national union officer who led a tempo band.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Why bandleaders are pushed to sing
segments.summary: Love says every bandleader is pressed to sing; Fields recalls Nat Cole's advice and Love praises In The Mood.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Billboard review of the Rainbow Ballroom, Denver, November 1941
segments.summary: Love reads a 1941 Billboard review of Fields' first colored band engagement at the Rainbow, noting instrumentation and soloists, and recalls meeting Fields that day.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Orchestra World clippings, a night with Basie, and the 1940s band polls
segments.summary: Love reads clippings and a Chicago poll that put Fields among the top ten black bands, ahead of Earl Hines and Andy Kirk.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Meeting his wife Bernice at a food show
segments.summary: Love asks about his marriage; Fields met Bernice Copeland when Ella Latimore introduced her, and learned she had been a Taft baby he had once admired.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Courtship and marriage around 1936-38
segments.summary: After about five years of courting while on the road, Bernice told him she was tired of waiting and they married.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Bernice's support and trust while he travelled
segments.summary: She backed him when the Hammond contract came and never worried about his road life, and welcomed every friend.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Raising Ernie Jr. and Carmen; Carmen on the road
segments.summary: Junior got a music scholarship but went to Howard; Carmen travelled with him and was hurt by segregated seating.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Carmen Fields gets a job at the Boston Globe
segments.summary: His daughter, a Lincoln University graduate, wins a Globe job by challenging the editor, and rises to assistant editor.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Carmen's move to television and family visits
segments.summary: She leaves the Globe for a Boston TV station and Fields visits her and Chief.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Ernie Jr.'s Jade Sound production company
segments.summary: Junior's Hollywood production company, backed by Rene Hall, offers recording, arranging and contracting services.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: The family's distances and why they won't move
segments.summary: Carmen works in Boston and Junior in Los Angeles; Fields and his wife stay in Tulsa.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Ernie Jr. rehearses an eighty-five-piece band for a young Black conductor
segments.summary: Junior rounds up musicians in the union hall to proof a young conductor's music for the Hollywood Symphony.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Marshal Royal and carrying every instrument to L.A. sessions
segments.summary: Junior was helped by Marshal Royal; session players must bring every instrument; Carmen refused to be a musician.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Reg Marshall as booking agent: Los Angeles dates and the 5-4 Ballroom
segments.summary: Reg Marshall got Fields into the Club Alabam after Kenton, the 5-4 Ballroom and Vancouver; Fields thought him honest because he wasn't big enough to cheat.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Dishonest booking practices of the Shaw Agency and Joe Glaser
segments.summary: He caught the Shaw agency in split commissions and notes how Glaser protected Hampton's interests.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: The best soloists in his band: Amos Woodruff, Booker Ervin and Luther West
segments.summary: Melvin Moore was the top singer; for solos he names Amos Woodruff, then Booker Ervin and Luther West.

segments.chapter: Theatres, family, rankings and opinions
segments.title: Russell 'Big Chief' Moore, Louis Armstrong and Jack Teagarden
segments.summary: Fields names Chief as the best all-round player; Armstrong told him nobody plays like Chief, but Teagarden had the name.

segments.chapter: Final years and closing reflections
segments.title: When he stopped travelling as a bandleader
segments.summary: Fields says his last year as a travelling bandleader was about 1965 and that he then took society dates near home.

segments.chapter: Final years and closing reflections
segments.title: Backing Sam Cooke for Don Robey and learning of his death
segments.summary: Robey's office hires Fields' band for Sam Cooke dates after Rene Hall vouches for him; on the road in West Texas he hears Cooke was shot, ending that hope for Junior.

segments.chapter: Final years and closing reflections
segments.title: Missing the band, and young fans at Ziegfeld's
segments.summary: Booking keeps him close to young musicians; at Ziegfeld's Basie salutes him and young people swarm his table.

segments.chapter: Final years and closing reflections
segments.title: The Teaspoon booking: a rock group, bad cars and a small-claims suit
segments.summary: Fields books a local rock group for a Fort Smith date, the cars break down, the promoter pays little, and the group sues in small-claims court.

segments.chapter: Final years and closing reflections
segments.title: His present booking: California Malibus, The Joker Is Wild and ABC
segments.summary: He books the self-contained California Malibus and an Oklahoma City group, and works occasionally with Associated Booking.

segments.chapter: Final years and closing reflections
segments.title: Ernie Jr.'s dispute with Bobby Bland's management
segments.summary: Junior led Bobby Bland's band, sued over unpaid money and hit union and management complications; Fields wishes he had taught him the union ways.

segments.chapter: Final years and closing reflections
segments.title: Tapes and photographs to send to Rutgers
segments.summary: Fields promises tapes, pictures and booking records for the project, and Love says eight and a half hours were recorded.

segments.chapter: Final years and closing reflections
segments.title: Hearing the great southwest bands, 1926-37, to learn musicians
segments.summary: He explains he developed his ear for musicians by listening to Dallas, Oklahoma City, Tulsa and Kansas City bands like Gene Coy, Buster Smith and Booker Pitman.

segments.chapter: Final years and closing reflections
segments.title: Trent's band, Lee Hilliard, Godley and the Smiths of Tulsa
segments.summary: He recalls Trent's players Lee Hilliard, A.G. Godley, Henry Smith and his son Geechee Smith, and Bostic and West as peers.

segments.chapter: Final years and closing reflections
segments.title: The Douglas Brothers, Paul Quinichette and Elon Watkins
segments.summary: Kansas City's Douglas brothers epitomized the local style but stayed home, as did Elon Watkins after Hampton raided Fields' band.

segments.chapter: Final years and closing reflections
segments.title: Decline of jazz standards among today's players
segments.summary: Love and Fields lament that today's fusion and avant-garde players lack the ability and standards of the old pool of musicians.

segments.chapter: Final years and closing reflections
segments.title: Basie's later years, Mercer Ellington's band and a corrupted era
segments.summary: Love laments Basie playing out his days and the Ellington name passed to Mercer, and both note how commercialization lowered standards.

segments.chapter: Final years and closing reflections
segments.title: Closing: news release and signing off
segments.summary: They ask Ron to send a news release, Fields tells how to label pictures, and Love signs off at 5:07 P.M. on November 1, 1981.
